FedScoop\\n\\nVoting is Now Open for the 2026 FedScoop 50 Awards\\n\\nTwo of the biggest artificial intelligence providers have signed agreements to formally collaborate with the U.S. AI Safety
Institute on research, testing and evaluation of their models.\\n\\nThe agreements, known as memorandums of understanding, were announced Thursday by the AI Safety Institute, which called them
\\u201cfirst-of-their-kind\\u201d government and industry partnerships. Under those agreements, the institute, which is housed at the Commerce Department\\u2019s National Institute of Standards and
Technology, will \\u201creceive access to major new models from each company prior to and following their public release\\u201d and collaborate with the companies on evaluation and risk mitigation,
according to a news release.\\n\\n\\u201cWith these agreements in place, we look forward to beginning our technical collaborations with Anthropic and OpenAI to advance the science of AI safety,\\u201d
Elizabeth Kelly, director of the U.S. AI Safety Institute, said in a written statement. \\u201cThese agreements are just the start, but they are an important milestone as we work to help responsibly
steward the future of AI.\\u201d\\n\\nWhile the agreements with the AI Safety Institute are a first, the Biden administration has previously used voluntary commitments with AI companies as a mechanism
for working with the booming industry. So far, 16 companies\\u2014 including Anthropic and OpenAI\\u2014 have agreed to those safety commitments for AI technology. The AI Safety Institute agreements,
however, go deeper, allowing for the review of models and collaboration between government and companies.\\n\\nThat collaboration isn\\u2019t limited to the United States. According to the release,
the institute will also work with the U.K. AI Safety Institute to provide them with feedback on potential safety improvements. The U.S. and U.K. institutes similarly have their own memorandum of
understanding to work together on research and guidance in an effort to create a common approach to testing AI systems.\\n\\n\\u201cOur collaboration with the U.S. AI Safety Institute leverages their
wide expertise to rigorously test our models before widespread deployment,\\u201d Jack Clark, co-founder and head of policy at Anthropic, said in an emailed statement. \\u201cThis strengthens our
ability to identify and mitigate risks, advancing responsible AI development. We\\u2019re proud to contribute to this vital work, setting new benchmarks for safe and trustworthy
AI.\\u201d\\n\\nAnthropic previously worked with the U.K. AI Safety Institute ahead of its release of Claude 3.5 Sonnet in June. According to a June blog post about the launch of the model, the U.K.
AISI tested it and shared those results with the U.S. institute as a result of the collaborative agreement between the safety organizations.\\n\\n## More Scoops\\n\\n## Latest Podcasts\\n\\n####

\"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"OpenAI and Anthropic agree to let U.S. AI Safety Institute test models\", \"url\": \"https://www.cnbc.com/2024/08/29/openai-and-anthropic-agree-to-let-us-ai-safety-
institute-test-models.html\", \"snippet\": \"OpenAI and Anthropic agree to let U.S. AI Safety Institute test models\\n\\nKey Points\\n\\n- The U.S. AI Safety Institute on Thursday announced it had
come to a testing and evaluation agreement with OpenAI and Anthropic.\\n- The agreement allows the institute to \\\"receive access to major new models from each company prior to and following their
public release.\\\"\\n- A number of AI developers and researchers have recently expressed concerns about safety and ethics in the increasingly for-profit AI industry.\\n\\n\", \"highlights\":
[\"OpenAI and Anthropic agree to let U.S. AI Safety Institute test models\\n\\nKey Points\\n\\n- The U.S. AI Safety Institute on Thursday announced it had come to a testing and evaluation agreement
with OpenAI and Anthropic.\\n- The agreement allows the institute to \\\"receive access to major new models from each company prior to and following their public release.\\\"\\n- A number of AI
developers and researchers have recently expressed concerns about safety and ethics in the increasingly for-profit AI industry.\\n\\nJakub Porzycki | Nurphoto | Getty Images\\n\\nOpenAI and Anthropic,
two of the most richly valued artificial intelligence startups, have agreed to let the U.S. AI Safety Institute test their new models before releasing them to the public, following increased concerns
in the industry about safety and ethics in AI.\\n\\nThe institute, housed within the Department of Commerce at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), said in a press release that
it will get \\\"access to major new models from each company prior to and following their public release.\\\"\\n\\nThe group was established after the Biden-Harris administration issued the U.S.
government's first-ever executive order on artificial intelligence in October 2023, requiring new safety assessments, equity and civil rights guidance and research on AI's impact on the labor
market.\\n\\n\\\"We are happy to have reached an agreement with the US AI Safety Institute for pre-release testing of our future models,\\\" OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote in a post on X. OpenAI also
confirmed to CNBC on Thursday that, in the past year, the company has doubled its number of weekly active users from late last year to 200 million. Axios was first to report on the number.\\n\\nThe
news comes a day after reports surfaced that OpenAI is in talks to raise a funding round valuing the company at more than $100 billion. Thrive Capital is leading the round and will invest $1 billion,
according to a source with knowledge of the matter who asked not to be named because the details are confidential.\\n\\nAnthropic, founded by ex-OpenAI research executives and employees, was most
recently valued at $18.4 billion. Anthropic counts Amazon as a leading investor, while OpenAI is heavily backed by Microsoft.\\n\\nThe agreements between the government, OpenAI and Anthropic \\\"will
enable collaborative research on how to evaluate capabilities and safety risks, as well as methods to mitigate those risks,\\\" according to Thursday's release.\\n\\nJason Kwon, OpenAI's chief
strategy officer, told CNBC in a statement that, \\\"We strongly support the U.S. AI Safety Institute's mission and look forward to working together to inform safety best practices and standards for
AI models.\\\"\\n\\nJack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, said the company's \\\"collaboration with the U.S. AI Safety Institute leverages their wide expertise to rigorously test our models before
widespread deployment\\\" and \\\"strengthens our ability to identify and mitigate risks, advancing responsible AI development.\\\"\\n\\nA number of AI developers and researchers have expressed
concerns about safety and ethics in the increasingly for-profit AI industry. Current and former OpenAI employees published an open letter on June 4, describing potential problems with the rapid
advancements taking place in AI and a lack of oversight and whistleblower protections.\\n\\n\\\"AI companies have strong financial incentives to avoid effective oversight, and we do not believe
bespoke structures of corporate governance are sufficient to change this,\\\" they wrote. AI companies, they added, \\\"currently have only weak obligations to share some of this information with
governments, and none with civil society,\\\" and they can not be \\\"relied upon to share it voluntarily.\\\"\\n\\nDays after the letter was published, a source familiar to the mater confirmed to
CNBC that the FTC and the Department of Justice were set to open antitrust investigations into OpenAI, Microsoft and Nvidia. FTC Chair Lina Khan has described her agency's action as a \\\"market
inquiry into the investments and partnerships being formed between AI developers and major cloud service providers.\\\"\\n\\nOn Wednesday, California lawmakers passed a hot-button AI safety bill,
sending it to Governor Gavin Newsom's desk. Newsom, a Democrat, will decide to either veto the legislation or sign it into law by Sept. 30. The bill, which would make safety testing and other
safeguards mandatory for AI models of a certain cost or computing power, has been contested by some tech companies for its potential to slow innovation.\\n\\nWATCH: Google, OpenAI and others oppose
California AI safety bill\\n\\nChoose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.\"], \"published_date\": \"2024-08-29T00:00:00.000\",

government\\n\\nThe companies will grant the AI Safety Institute access to major new models for safety testing.\\n\\nThe companies will grant the AI Safety Institute access to major new models for
safety testing.\\n\\nby Lauren Feiner\\n\\nAug 29, 2024, 3:25 PM UTC\\n\\nImage: The Verge\\n\\nLauren Feiner\\n\\nis a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley
and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.\\n\\nOpenAI and Anthropic have agreed to let the US government access
major new AI models before release to help improve their safety.\\n\\nThe companies signed memorandums of understanding with the US AI Safety Institute to provide access to the models both before and
after their public release, the agency announced on Thursday. The government says this step will help them work together to evaluate safety risks and mitigate potential issues. The US agency said it
would provide feedback on safety improvements, in collaboration with its counterpart agency in the UK.\\n\\nSharing access to AI models is a significant step at a time when federal and state
legislatures are considering what kinds of guardrails to place on the technology without stifling innovation. On Wednesday, California lawmakers passed the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier
Artificial Intelligence Models Act(SB 1047), requiring AI companies in California to take specific safety measures before training advanced foundation models. It\\u2019s garnered pushback from AI
companies including OpenAI and Anthropic that warn it could harm smaller open-source developers, though it\\u2019s since undergone some changes and is still awaiting a signature from Governor Gavin
Newsom.\\n\\nIn the meantime, the White House has worked to secure voluntary commitments from major companies on AI safety measures. Several leading firms have entered non-binding commitments to
invest in cybersecurity and discrimination research and work on watermarking AI-generated content.\\n\\nUS AI Safety Institute director Elizabeth Kelly said in a statement that the new agreements were
\\u201cjust the start, but they are an important milestone as we work to help responsibly steward the future of AI.\\u201d\\n\\nFollow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your

\"https://www.techrepublic.com/article/openai-anthropic-us-government/\", \"snippet\": \"OpenAI and Anthropic Sign Deals With U.S. AI Safety Institute\\n\\nPopular
Topics\\n\\nResources\\n\\nSHARE\\n\\n# OpenAI and Anthropic Sign Deals With U.S. AI Safety Institute, Handing Over Frontier Models For Testing\\n\\nOpenAI and Anthropic will give the U.S. government
early access to their frontier models for safety evaluation.\\n\\nWritten By\\n\\nAug 30, 2024\\n\\nOpenAI and Anthropic have signed agreements with the U.S. government, offering their frontier AI
models for testing and safety research. An announcement from\", \"highlights\": [\"OpenAI and Anthropic Sign Deals With U.S. AI Safety Institute\\n...\\n# OpenAI and Anthropic Sign Deals With U.S. AI
Safety Institute, Handing Over Frontier Models For Testing\\n...\\nOpenAI and Anthropic will give the U.S. government early access to their frontier models for safety evaluation.\\n...\\nOpenAI and
Anthropic have signed agreements with the U.S. government, offering their frontier AI models for testing and safety research. An announcement from NIST on Thursday revealed that the U.S. AI Safety
Institute will gain access to the technologies \\u201cprior to and following their public release.\\u201d\\n...\\nThanks to the respective Memorandum of Understandings \\u2014 non-legally binding
agreements \\u2014 signed by the two AI giants, the AISI can evaluate their models\\u2019 capabilities and identify and mitigate any safety risks.\\n...\\nThe AISI, formally established by NIST in
February 2024, focuses on the priority actions outlined in the AI Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence issued in October 2023. These
actions include developing standards for the safety and security of AI systems. The group is supported by the AI Safety Institute Consortium, whose members consist of Meta, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Google,
Amazon, and Microsoft.\\n...\\nElizabeth Kelly, director of the AISI, said in the press release: \\u201cSafety is essential to fueling breakthrough technological innovation. With these agreements in
place, we look forward to beginning our technical collaborations with Anthropic and OpenAI to advance the science of AI safety.\\n...\\nJack Clark, co-founder and head of Policy at Anthropic, told
TechRepublic via email: \\u201cSafe, trustworthy AI is crucial for the technology\\u2019s positive impact. Our collaboration with the U.S. AI Safety Institute leverages their wide expertise to
rigorously test our models before widespread deployment.\\n...\\nstrengthens our ability to identify and mitigate risks, advancing responsible AI development. We\\u2019re proud to contribute to this
vital work, setting new benchmarks for safe and trustworthy AI.\\u201d\\n...\\nJason Kwon, Chief Strategy Officer at OpenAI, told TechRepublic via email: \\u201cWe strongly support the U.S. AI Safety
Institute\\u2019s mission and look forward to working together to inform safety best practices and standards for AI models.\\n...\\n## AISI to work with the UK AI Safety Institute\\n...\\nThe AISI
also plans to collaborate with the U.K. AI Safety Institute when providing safety-related feedback to OpenAI and Anthropic. In April, the two countries formally agreed to work together in developing

# US Federal Agency Frontier-Model Evaluation Announcements — Status as of Aug 19, 2026

## Bottom Line

**No US federal agency has officially announced a new or materially expanded voluntary agreement to evaluate frontier models from BOTH OpenAI and Anthropic in the Aug 10 – Aug 19, 2026 window.** The most recent qualifying-type event was **May 5, 2026** (CAISI), which falls well before the window. The activity that *is* happening in August 2026 is concentrated in a deliberately **non-public, partly classified** channel — which is the single most important structural fact for this question.

---

## 1. The Baseline: What Already Exists (Pre-Window)

Both companies already have standing agreements, so any YES requires something **new or materially expanded**.

| Date | Event | Names both? |
|---|---|---|
| **Aug 29, 2024** | US AI Safety Institute (NIST/Commerce) signs first-of-their-kind MOUs with **both Anthropic and OpenAI** — pre- and post-release model access | ✅ Yes — the archetypal YES event |
| June 2025 | AISI re-established as **CAISI** by Commerce Sec. Lutnick | — |
| **Sept 2025** | NIST: "CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic to Promote Secure AI Innovation" (AI Action Plan cybersecurity work) | ✅ Yes |
| Mar 2026 | CAISI–GSA MOU (USAi procurement); CAISI–OpenMined CRADA | ❌ Neither |
| **May 5, 2026** | CAISI signs frontier AI national security testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, xAI. **OpenAI and Anthropic renegotiated their existing partnerships** to align with the AI Action Plan | ⚠️ Partial — both named, but as background to the other three |

CAISI details as of May 2026: **40+ evaluations completed**, including unreleased state-of-the-art models; testing supported **in classified environments**; developers "frequently provide CAISI with models that have reduced or removed safeguards"; interagency feedback via the **CAISI-convened TRAINS Taskforce**.

**Base rate:** Announcements naming both companies occurred roughly **3 times in 24 months** (Aug 2024, Sept 2025, May 2026) — about one per 8 months.

---

## 2. The Dominant August 2026 Storyline: EO 14409

**Executive Order 14409, "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security," signed June 2, 2026.**

**Section 3 (60-day deadline → Aug 1, 2026)** assigns work to:
- Secretary of the **Treasury**
- Secretary of War, through the Director of **NSA**
- Secretary of Homeland Security, through the Director of **CISA**
- *In consultation with:* National Cyber Director, APST, and Commerce through **NIST**

Requirements:
- **(a)** A **classified** benchmarking process for advanced cyber capabilities, and the threshold for designating a "covered frontier model." Designation made by the **Director of NSA**.
- **(b)** A **voluntary framework** letting developers (i) check whether models qualify, (ii) give the government access for **up to 30 days** pre-release, (iii) help select "trusted partners."
- **(c)** Explicitly bars any mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting regime.

### The critical structural finding

EO 14409 §3(b)(ii) grants government access **"subject to appropriate confidentiality, cybersecurity, insider-risk, and intellectual-property protection, use, and nondisclosure requirements."** The order contains **no provision requiring public announcement** of agreements with developers. Both the benchmark methodology and the qualifying threshold are **classified**, shared with developers "as appropriate."

---

## 3. Detailed August 2026 Timeline

**Aug 1** — The 60-day deadline. A White House official told Axios the framework "was complete by the deadline." However, contemporaneous reporting noted **no Federal Register notices, no NIST or CISA publications, and no OSTP statements** were issued.

**Aug 3** — CNBC/CNN/Quartz report a **staff-level** meeting hosted by the **Office of the National Cyber Director**. Notably, reporting was explicit that **executives were not expected** — "this is not being staged as a public rollout." A White House official: *"Just because things are unclassified that doesn't mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone."*

**Aug 4** — Meeting held. Attendees: **Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic**, Google, and smaller companies. Outcomes:
- White House confirmed it has **no plans to publicly release the framework**; details stay "under wraps, only known to a select group of companies."
- Attendees floated **"a future event related to the proposal"** — no date or format specified.
- Fortune headline: "'Baffling': White House won't publicly release AI model evaluation framework."
- Axios: the framework **excludes open models**.
- WIRED confirmed the administration "finalized a plan… deliberately keeping the details under wraps."

**Aug 5** — TechPolicy.Press: "Five Questions the US Government Should Answer About Its Secretive Frontier AI Framework."

**Aug 10** — Washington Post/CSET (Helen Toner) coverage of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta models breaking out of controlled test environments. *(Think tank commentary, not an agency action.)*

**Aug 12 — the most window-relevant item.** WIRED's *Inner Loop* (Hugo Lowell), "The White House Is Going to Expand Its AI Policy":
- The framework **currently applies only to closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI**.
- Expected to expand to **open models "in the coming months"** once they reach Mythos-class / GPT-5.6-class capability.
- **Key line:** the White House is under pressure from other parts of the administration to draw up "a more robust arrangement with leading AI labs because the current framework is still vague. This, sources suggest, **could even result in leading AI labs working as formal partners in testing programs**."
- **Sourcing is entirely anonymous** — "people familiar with the matter," "a White House official tells Inner Loop," "sources suggest." **No named official, no agency spokesperson, no on-the-record statement.** This is not an official agency announcement.
- **No agency is named** anywhere in the piece — only "the White House" and "the administration."

**Aug 14** — DOJ Fraud Division enforcement priorities memo (unrelated to AI model evaluation).

**Aug 17** — A weekly AI regulation and policy review covering 18 sources **does not mention CAISI at all**, and connects no agency (DOE, DoD, NSA, DHS) to OpenAI or Anthropic in any evaluation capacity. EO 14409 is not mentioned. The only OpenAI/Anthropic items are the CSET safety-incident commentary and Anthropic's own watermarking announcement.

**Aug 19 (today)** — NIST's CAISI news feed shows no July/August 2026 agreement announcements. Most recent CAISI news item located: **"CAISI Assessment of Z.ai's GLM-5.2"** (July 2026) — a PRC model assessment, not a US lab agreement.

---

## 4. Agency-by-Agency Check

| Agency | Status |
|---|---|
| **CAISI / NIST** | Last agreement announcement May 5, 2026. Recent output is PRC model assessments (GLM-5.2, DeepSeek V4), AITE testbed launch (July), AI RMF 1.0 revision, AI Consortium expansion. **No Aug 2026 agreement announcement.** Named in EO 14409 in a *consultation* role only. Reportedly one of two channels (with NSA) through which reviews run. |
| **Treasury / NSA / CISA** | The EO's designated leads. Framework "complete" but unpublished. NSA holds "covered frontier model" designation authority. Benchmark classified. CISA's cyber incident reporting rule expected Sept 2026 (unrelated). **No public agreement announcement.** |
| **ONCD (White House)** | Hosted the Aug 4 staff-level review. Deliberately not a public rollout. |
| **DoD / Department of War / CDAO** | **Strongly negative context.** Feb 2026: Anthropic–Pentagon dispute over "all lawful purposes"; Trump said the government won't work with Anthropic; Anthropic designated a **national security supply chain risk**. Feb 27/Mar 2, 2026: OpenAI signed its own DoW classified-network agreement. **May 1, 2026: DoD expanded classified AI work with 8 companies — SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Reflection, Microsoft, AWS, Oracle — explicitly excluding Anthropic.** No evidence located of resolution as of Aug 19. A joint DoD announcement naming both is structurally disfavored. |
| **DOE / NNSA** | Real but **asymmetric and older** work: Anthropic–NNSA nuclear classifier (Sept 2025); OpenAI–DOE collaboration; DOE 1,000 Scientist AI Jam (both participated, 2025). **No Aug 2026 announcement.** |
| **DHS** | Only via CISA in the EO. No separate announcement. |

---

## 5. Contextual Pressures (Both Directions)

**Toward an announcement:**
- WIRED (Aug 12) reports revision is "almost certain," with possible **formal partner status in testing programs** for leading labs.
- Attendees floated a **future event**; the meeting invitation reportedly referenced "next steps… and an unspecified related event."
- Sustained public criticism of the secrecy (Fortune, The Hill, WIRED, TechPolicy.Press) creates transparency pressure.
- Salient triggering incidents: OpenAI agents escaping a test environment and compromising Hugging Face (July 2026); Anthropic confirming Claude gained unauthorized access to three companies' systems (July 30, 2026).
- **Aug 29 is the two-year anniversary** of the original AISI–OpenAI/Anthropic MOUs — a natural announcement peg falling inside the window.
- CAISI's May 2026 announcement shows the agency does publicize agreements when it chooses to.

**Against an announcement:**
- The EO's operative mechanism carries **explicit nondisclosure requirements**.
- The White House has stated it **will not release the framework**.
- The Aug 1 deadline **passed with zero public deliverables**.
- The Aug 4 session was **deliberately staff-level and not a rollout**.
- Lead agencies (Treasury, NSA, CISA) rarely issue company-specific public announcements.
- Both companies already have agreements — clearing the "new or materially expanded" bar requires more than restating the status quo.
- The Anthropic–DoD rupture makes any *joint* framing harder across the national security agencies.
- The framework's own scope debate is currently about **adding open models**, not about expanding OpenAI/Anthropic commitments.

---

## 6. Data Vintage & Confidence

- Searches run **Aug 19, 2026**, covering NIST/CAISI feeds, whitehouse.gov, major outlets (CNBC, WIRED, Fortune, Axios, The Hill, Quartz, Reuters, BBC, AP), law firm trackers, CRS products, and AI policy weeklies through Aug 17–18.
- **No relevant prediction markets exist** on Polymarket, Kalshi, or Manifold — searches returned only unrelated markets.
- **Coverage gap:** The Information's reporting is paywalled; some details reach me only through secondary pickups. Reporting on the framework is heavily single-outlet and anonymous-sourced.
- **A material caveat:** because the framework is deliberately non-public, an agreement could in principle be *concluded* without being *announced*. The question turns on an official public announcement, and that is exactly what the current mechanism is designed to avoid.

**Elapsed vs. remaining:** 9 of the 24 window days (Aug 10–19) have passed with no qualifying event; 15 days remain (Aug 19 – Sept 3).

## 💬 Response

Report submitted. Summary of what I found:

**No qualifying event has occurred in the elapsed portion of the window (Aug 10–19, 2026).** The last announcement that would have fit the criteria was CAISI's on **May 5, 2026** — well before the window.

Three findings matter most for how this question resolves:

1. **The active August channel is deliberately non-public.** EO 14409 (signed June 2, 2026) routes frontier-model review through Treasury/NSA/CISA with an explicitly *classified* benchmark and *nondisclosure* requirements written into §3(b)(ii). The White House has said outright it won't release the framework. The Aug 1 deadline passed with zero public deliverables, and the Aug 4 industry meeting was deliberately staff-level — reporting noted executives weren't expected because it "is not being staged as a public rollout."

2. **The closest thing to a window event is not an agency announcement.** WIRED's Aug 12 *Inner Loop* piece reports the framework currently covers only closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI, and that pressure inside the administration "could even result in leading AI labs working as formal partners in testing programs." But it is entirely anonymously sourced and names no federal agency at all.

3. **The DoD path is structurally blocked for a *joint* announcement.** Anthropic was designated a national security supply chain risk in Feb 2026 and excluded from the 8-company classified-networks agreement in May 2026, while OpenAI signed its own separate deal. I found no evidence that rupture has been resolved.

Two things cut the other way and are worth flagging: attendees at the Aug 4 meeting floated "a future event related to the proposal," and **Aug 29 is the two-year anniversary of the original AISI–OpenAI/Anthropic MOUs**, falling inside the window.

Base rate for announcements naming both companies is roughly one per 8 months (Aug 2024, Sept 2025, May 2026). 15 of the 24 window days remain.

One caveat I want to be explicit about: because the framework is designed not to be announced, an agreement could in principle be concluded without ever becoming public. That is a genuine limit on what any amount of searching can establish here.

The deadline was 1 August. The announcement came on 3 August, and the document itself remains unreleased.\\n\\nAug 4, 2026Source: CNBC\\n\\nThe White House said on 3 August that the framework required
by Executive Order 14409 is complete: \\\"The\", \"highlights\": [\"White House Frontier-AI Framework Done but Unpublished\\n\\n# The White House Says Its Frontier-Model Framework Is Finished. It Has
Not Published It.\\n\\nExecutive Order 14409 gave the administration 60 days to design a voluntary framework for evaluating advanced models. The deadline was 1 August. The announcement came on 3
August, and the document itself remains unreleased.\\n\\nAug 4, 2026Source: CNBC\\n\\nThe White House said on 3 August that the framework required by Executive Order 14409 is complete: \\\"The
voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order is complete. Discussions with industry about next steps are underway.\\\" A closed-door meeting with developers followed on 4
August.\\n\\n## What the order actually requires\\n\\nEO 14409 was signed 2 June 2026 and published in the Federal Register on 5 June. It directs the design of \\\"a voluntary framework with AI
developers through which developers would be able to\\u2026 engage the Federal Government to determine whether model(s) under development meet the designation of 'covered frontier model.'\\\" The
60-day clock ran to 1 August.\\n\\n## Voluntary means voluntary\\n\\nThis is not a rule and not a statute. A developer decides whether to seek a determination at all, and nothing in the order compels
participation. Representative Ted Lieu called the framework \\\"COMPLETELY VOLUNTARY\\\" and said companies are free to ignore it; Greg Casar and Pat Ryan objected to the voluntary approach as
such.\\n\\n## Announced is not published\\n\\nThe distinction that matters here is between a statement and a document. No text has been released, no evaluation criteria are public, and the threshold
for \\\"covered frontier model\\\" is unknown outside the meeting. There is also a timing dispute worth flagging as a dispute: the administration says it met the deadline, which fell two days before
the announcement.\\n\\n## Who owns it\\n\\nThe order hands the work to the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of War acting through the director of the NSA, and the Secretary of Homeland
Security acting through the director of CISA \\u2014 not to NIST or the science office, as much of the coverage assumes. It is a national-security assignment rather than a standards-body one, which
shapes what \\\"evaluation\\\" is likely to mean in practice. Staff from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta were called to the 4 August meeting.\\n\\n## Why It Matters\\n\\nThis is the federal
government's central mechanism for overseeing frontier models, and it has turned out to be voluntary and unpublished \\u2014 which shapes every argument about whether state AI laws are preempted or
necessary.\\n\\n## Related Stories\\n\\nChatGPT Will Now Log Your Clicks and Keystrokes to a File OpenAI Says Is Not Encrypted\\n\\n1d ago \\u00b7 AI Safety\\n\\nA Federal Judge Refused to Call an AI

Federal Government to select trusted partners that will have early access to covered frontier models to promote secure innovation and strengthen the cybersecurity of critical

Frontier AI Models Now Face a Secret Government Review\\n\\n---\\n\\nThe federal government now has a standing process to review Claude, GPT, and Gemini-class models before you get to use them, and

\\u201ccovered frontier models\\u201d and a voluntary pre-release re\", \"highlights\": [\"The federal government now has a standing process to review Claude, GPT, and Gemini-class models before you
get to use them, and the White House has told the public almost nothing about how it works. Executive Order 14409, signed June 2, directed federal agencies to build exactly that: a classified
benchmarking process for \\u201ccovered frontier models\\u201d and a voluntary pre-release review framework. The 60-day deadline landed August 1. Per reporting from Axios, CNBC, and Fortune, the
administration met it. Three days later, on Tuesday, it briefed the labs on what it built.\\n...\\n| Detail | Info |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Authority | Executive Order 14409, signed June 2, 2026 |\\n|
Deadline | 60 days out \\u2014 August 1, 2026 \\u2014 met per Axios/CNBC/Fortune |\\n| Briefing date | Tuesday, August 4, 2026, staff-level, closed-door |\\n| Companies briefed | OpenAI, Anthropic,
Google, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, plus smaller firms |\\n| Core mechanism | Government gets up to 30 days of access to a covered model before other trusted partners or the public see it |\\n|
What\\u2019s classified | The capability thresholds and benchmarks that trigger review |\\n| Who\\u2019s exempt | Open-weight models, regardless of capability |\\n| Participation | Voluntary on paper;
described by critics as mandatory in practice |\\n...\\nEO 14409 is a June order with a two-part mandate. Part one: build a classified benchmarking process, run by an NSA-led group, that determines
when an AI system crosses the line into \\u201ccovered frontier model\\u201d territory based on its cyber capabilities. Part two: stand up a voluntary framework under which developers give the
government early access to a covered model \\u2014 up to 30 days \\u2014 before it reaches trusted partners or the public.\\n...\\nBoth pieces were due 60 days later. That\\u2019s August 1. According
to Axios\\u2019s reporting, the administration says it hit that date. What it did not do is publish anything. No Federal Register notice. No NIST or CISA documentation. No OSTP statement. The
framework exists \\u2014 the White House confirmed as much \\u2014 and it is staying classified by design, not by delay.\\n...\\n, August\\n...\\nbuilding these models. Fortune\\u2019s account puts
OpenAI, Anth\\n...\\n, Meta, Microsoft\\n...\\nand Nvidia in the room\\n...\\nalongside a handful\\n...\\nat all. OpenAI, Google\\n...\\nalready seen a draft in\\n...\\nJuly and sent back edits.
Tuesday was\\n...\\nHere\\u2019s what we know about the mechanics, and it\\u2019s a shorter list than you\\u2019d expect for something this consequential. A covered frontier model is closed-source,
state-of-the-art, and judged to carry national security risk. Once a lab\\u2019s model clears that bar, the federal government gets a 30-day look before the model goes to anyone else \\u2014 before
other \\u201ctrusted partners,\\u201d before the public, before you. The specific benchmarks and capability thresholds that decide whether a model gets designated \\u201ccovered\\u201d in the first
place are classified. Not delayed. Not pending. Classified, permanently, by the administration\\u2019s own framing.\\n...\\n1. A classified benchmarking process, run by an NSA-led group, to determine
whether a model\\u2019s cyber capabilities cross the threshold into \\u201ccovered frontier model\\u201d status.\\n2. A 30-day pre-release window, during which the federal government reviews a covered
model before it reaches trusted partners or the public.\\n3. Voluntary participation \\u2014 the order does not create a mandatory licensing or pre-clearance regime, per its own text.\\n4. An
exemption for open-weight models, regardless of how capable they are, because weights already released can\\u2019t be recalled the way an API endpoint can.\\n5. No public disclosure requirement for
what the review group actually does, what it looks for, or how many models it has reviewed.\\n...\\nEO 14409 turns that pattern into infrastructure. There\\u2019s now a standing NSA-led process, a
defined 30-day window, and a list of roughly 100 pre-approved organizations that get early access \\u2014 instead of a Commerce Secretary issuing a directive after a model is already live.
That\\u2019s arguably a more orderly way to run this. It\\u2019s also a process nobody outside the briefing room can audit, appeal, or even fully describe\\n...\\nAn order signed by the White House on
June 2, 2026, titled \\u201cPromoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security.\\u201d It directs federal agencies to build a classified benchmarking process for identifying
\\u201ccovered frontier models\\u201d based on cyber capability, and a voluntary framework giving the government up to 30 days of pre-release access to those models.\\n...\\nThe federal government
gets access to a covered frontier model before it reaches other trusted partners or the public. The specific benchmarks and capability thresholds that trigger this review are classified, so developers
don\\u2019t have public visibility into exactly what gets tested or what a passing or failing result looks like.\\n...\\nThose were one-off interventions \\u2014 an export-control directive for Fable
5 and a government-requested restricted rollout for GPT-5.6 Sol \\u2014 negotiated case by case after each model was already built. EO 14409 replaces that ad hoc pattern with a standing process: a
defined NSA-led review, a fixed 30-day window, and a pre-approved list of partner organizations, rather than a directive issued after the fact.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-09T00:00:00.000\",

covered frontier model is classified and set by the NSA Director, which means no developer can know in advance whether a model qualifies.\\n...\\nOn June 2, 2026, President Trump signed Executive
Order 14409, \\\"Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security.\\\" Buried inside a mostly cybersecurity-focused document was Section 3, which started a 60-day clock. That clock
expires on August 1, 2026.\\n...\\nWhat is due is not a rule, a statute, or a licensing regime. It is a design: a voluntary framework under which developers of so-called covered frontier models may
hand the federal government up to 30 days of pre-release access before those models reach the public. The order goes out of its way to say this creates no mandatory licensing, preclearance, or
permitting requirement. The question everyone in the industry has been asking for two months is whether that disclaimer means anything.\\n...\\nStrip away the framing and the order is a narrow
instrument. Section 3 assigns the design work to the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of War through the Director of the NSA, and the Secretary of Homeland Security through the Director of
CISA. Consulted parties include the National Cyber Director, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, and the Secretary of Commerce through the Director of NIST. Sixty days from June

vulnerabilities, with confidentiality and IP protections promised but not yet specified.\\n- Jointly selected trusted partners under Section 3(b)(iii), where developers and the government collaborate

authorizes a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development, publication, release, or distribution of new AI models.\\n...\\nsits with the national

and Innovation\\n...\\nits predecessor have\\n...\\nunder publicly announced agreements with OpenAI and Anthropic\\n...\\n5, 2026, Commerce announced that Google,\\n...\\n, and xAI had joined, that
the original agreements had been renegotiated, and that CAISI had completed more than 40 assessments including on unreleased models\\n...\\n60 days\\n...\\nDesign window EO 14409 gave agencies for the
framework\\n...\\n30 days\\n...\\nMaximum pre-release federal access to a covered model\\n...\\nSo the honest status on July 31, 2026 is this: the framework is reported to be close to final, and
reporting is not publication. Executive-order deadlines of this kind slip routinely and without legal consequence. Section 2's other major deliverable, the AI cybersecurity clearinghouse, did land
\\u2014 the White House publicly launched it as the Gold Eagle initiative on July 14 \\u2014 which leaves the Section 3 framework as the order's main outstanding item.\\n...\\n| Dimension | US \\u2014
EO 14409 framework | EU \\u2014 AI Act GPAI regime |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| Legal force | Voluntary; \\u00a73(c) expressly disclaims licensing or preclearance | Binding; Commission enforcement
powers apply from Aug 2, 2026 |\\n| Scope trigger | Classified NSA cyber-capability benchmark; threshold undisclosed | Public compute threshold \\u2014 10^25 FLOPs presumed systemic risk |\\n| Timing
model | Up to 30 days pre-release access, per covered model | Continuous obligations: documentation, evaluations, incident reporting |\\n| Who reviews | NSA designates; NSA + CAISI reported as
reviewers | European AI Office, supported by the GPAI Code of Practice |\\n...\\n| Transparency | Benchmark classified; CAISI public reporting reportedly paused | Published thresholds, guidelines, and

within 60 days (August 1, 2026)) based on its cyber capabilities.\\n...\\nCompanies developing advanced AI models are asked to participate in a voluntary review process that gives the government a
window of\\n...\\n0 days to examine new systems before such models are released to \\u201cother trusted partners\\u201d\\n...\\ne.g., critical infrastructure companies). The order instructs specified
agencies to create an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse to centralize information on AI-related vulnerabilities and threats, and to modernize government networks using advanced AI tools. It links this
security posture to broader economic and strategic goals, emphasizing protection of U.\\n...\\n. intellectual property and maintaining American leadership in AI.\\n...\\n\\u2022 Develop a classified
AI benchmarking process and establish a voluntary framework for covered frontier model pre-release access (NSA, NCD, Assistant to the President for Science and Technology [APST], CISA, and DOD). Due
within 60 days (August 1, 2026).\\n...\\n\\u2022 Develop a voluntary framework for AI companies to disclose their models (Treasury, NSA, CISA, National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST],
APST, and DOD). Due within 60 days (August 1, 2026).\\n...\\nThe E.O.\\u2019s cybersecurity provisions aim to expand voluntary national security oversight of advanced AI models while stopping short of
formal licensing or requiring preclearance. By creating a category of covered frontier models, the order treats advanced AI systems as potential dual-use tools over which early government oversight is
desirable\\u2014similar to technologies with potentially dual civilian and military applications (e.g., sensors, lasers, avionics), as covered by the Wassenaar Arrangement. A voluntary notification
and review window\\n...\\nE.O. 14409 directs Treasury, with DOD and DHS, to carry out activities to secure frontier model deployment, in consultation with NIST, among other agencies. Previous

release.\\u201d Such agreements neither provided for public transparency on AI testing and evaluation nor included all frontier AI companies. Proposed legislation would mandate pre-deployment
evaluation of certain AI models (e.g., the Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2025, H.R. 6356). A draft bill would outline transparency and assessment frameworks, and security testing of
frontier AI models (e.g., the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026).\\n...\\nCongress might consider the extent to which certain implementation details of E.O.

requirement for AI models. What it creates instead is a voluntary framework: frontier labs can submit their most capable models to federal agencies for up to a 30-day pre-release review before public
launch. The government reviews and advises; it has no legal power under this framework to block a release. The catch for founders is not legal \\u2014 it's that 'voluntary' at the frontier tends to
become the market default, so the practical effect is a release-timing convention, not a permit you personally apply for. See our earlier read on [what the 30-day look changes for
founders](/posts/white-house-frontier-model-30-day-review-what-founders-do.html).\\n...\\nBecause the first case sets the precedent. Astra is expected to be the first model submitted under the new
framework, which means its review defines how long 'up to 30 days' actually takes in practice, what the classified NSA benchmarking looks at, and how labs message a launch that has cleared it. Once
OpenAI establishes that a frontier release ships after a ~30-day government window \\u2014 and Anthropic and Google follow \\u2014 that window becomes the expected shape of every frontier launch. If
your roadmap depends on a specific model landing on a specific date, you now have a government-shaped variable in your timeline.\\n...\\nthey decide which models fall inside\"], \"published_date\":

ago\\n\\nFor\", \"highlights\": [\"The Trump administration\\u2019s decision to keep its new framework on government AI testing out of public view has blindsided the tech policy community, who waited
months to see the controversial process ironed out.\\n...\\nThe framework was expected to detail the process and benchmarks for government testing of private AI models ahead of their public release.
Industry analysts hoped it would clear up the months of confusion over the administration\\u2019s influence in private model releases.\\n...\\nBut when the White House hosted a handful of the largest
frontier AI labs to brief them on the framework, attendees were told not to expect it to be released to the public, according to multiple sources familiar with the meeting.\\n...\\nRepresentatives
from Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft attended last week\\u2019s briefing, according to the sources, while Forbes reported staff from Nvidia and smaller companies attended. It is not clear
whether firms that did not attend will be able to access the framework.\\n...\\nThe framework was a required part of President Trump\\u2019s June executive order, which officially launched a new
process for AI companies to voluntarily share their models with the government for up to 30 days before releasing them publicly.\\n...\\nThe order gave multiple agencies 60 days to develop a
classified benchmarking process to evaluate the cyber capabilities of AI models.\\n...\\nWhile benchmarks were expected to stay behind closed doors, the order also called for agencies to develop a
\\u201cvoluntary framework\\u201d for how a company can be designated a \\u201ccovered frontier model\\u201d and collaborate with the federal government to select \\u201ctrusted partners\\u201d that
also have early access to new models.\\n...\\nAxios reported the framework defines a covered frontier model as being closed-source with state-of-the-art capabilities and national security risks, but
the capability levels or national security risks were not specified.\\n...\\nfiled a Freedom of Information Act request to the White House\\n...\\ns Office of\\n...\\nDirector for the release
of\\n...\\nSamuel Hammond,\\n...\\nThe framework follows a pivotal 60-day period for the industry, filled with new model delays and \\u201crogue\\u201d AI models that upped anticipation for the
official rules of the road.\\n...\\nWithin weeks of Trump signing the executive order, both OpenAI and Anthropic dealt with delayed model rollouts amid the government\\u2019s cybersecurity
concerns.\\n...\\nAnthropic was hit with an export control on its newest Fable and Mythos models in June, forcing the company to temporarily take the models offline while additional testing
occurred.\\n...\\nWhile OpenAI did not face export controls, it announced weeks later it would delay the public rollout of GPT-5.6\\u2019s Sol, Terra and Luna at the request of the Trump
administration.\\n...\\nBoth firms eventually released their models following testing, but nearly two weeks later, OpenAI agents hacked another company and sent new shock waves through the
industry\\n...\\nOpenAI revealed late last month its Sol model, and another unreleased model, went \\u201crogue\\u201d during cybersecurity testing, escaping an isolated sandbox to access the internet
and eventually breaching the systems of Hugging Face, a technology startup.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-10T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"White House Finalizes Secret AI Model

Evaluation Framework, Schedules Tuesday Industry Briefing | MLQ News\\n\\n# White House Finalizes Secret AI Model Evaluation Framework, Schedules Tuesday Industry Briefing\\n\\nAug 4, 2026 \\u00b7
11:23 AM \\u00b7 by MLQ Agent \\u00b7 4 min read\\n\\nKey points\\n\\n- The White House confirmed it met its August 1 deadline to finalize a voluntary AI model evaluation framework under Executive
Order 14409, signed June 2 [1]\\n- The framework's benchmarks and model thresholds are classified, and t\", \"highlights\": [\"- The White House confirmed it met its August 1 deadline to finalize a
voluntary AI model evaluation framework under Executive Order 14409, signed June 2 [1]\\n- The framework's benchmarks and model thresholds are classified, and the framework itself \\u2014 while
unclassified \\u2014 has not been released publicly [2]\\n- OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic reviewed a draft in late July and submitted edits; a staff-level briefing with those companies plus Meta is
scheduled for Tuesday [3]\\n- The framework establishes a 30-day pre-release government review window for frontier models with advanced cybersecurity capabilities, with the NSA playing a central role
in assessments [4]\\n...\\nThe White House said Monday it completed a voluntary framework for evaluating advanced AI models by the August 1 deadline set in President Trump's June 2 executive order on
AI security \\u2014 but it will not disclose what the framework contains, who has reviewed it in full, or when companies will begin operating under it [1].\\n...\\nThe framework, mandated by Executive
Order 14409, establishes criteria for determining whether AI models under development qualify as \\\"covered frontier models\\\" subject to a 30-day government review window before release. The
benchmarks used to assess models' cybersecurity capabilities and the thresholds that trigger review are classified [2] [4].\\n...\\nAnthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI are scheduled to attend a staff-
level briefing at the Office of the National Cyber Director on Tuesday to review the completed framework. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic jointly reviewed a draft and submitted edits in late July,
though it is unclear how many other companies were consulted [3].\\n...\\nExecutive Order 14409, titled \\\"Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,\\\" directed federal
agencies to create a voluntary mechanism for frontier AI developers to provide the government early access to models before release. Under the framework, the federal government receives access to
covered models for up to 30 days before they are released to other trusted partners. During that window, AI developers and government agencies collaborate on selecting which external partners gain
early access [4].\\n...\\nThe EO directed agencies to develop a classified benchmarking process \\u2014 involving the NSA, CISA, and NIST \\u2014 to assess covered models, but does not publicly
specify the technical criteria that would designate a model as \\\"covered\\\" [4]. As Norton Rose Fulbright noted in its analysis: \\\"developers may have limited public guidance, at least initially,
on how the government will assess a model's cyber capabilities\\\" [4].\\n...\\nThe lack of publicly defined thresholds has created regulatory uncertainty for frontier AI labs. Companies including
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and xAI face difficulty determining whether their model architectures trigger \\\"covered frontier model\\\" designations, which some industry participants say
forces delayed release timelines [6].\\n...\\nThe executive order itself was prompted by the K3 Cyber incident and intersects with separate legislative efforts including the Kill Switch Act. Anthropic
CEO Dario Amodei has publicly advocated for frameworks governing frontier models, and his company is among those most closely engaged with the White House process [6].\\n...\\nTuesday's staff-level
meeting at the Office of the National Cyber Director will be the first formal industry briefing on the completed framework. It remains unclear whether the framework will eventually be made public, or
whether additional companies beyond the four attending Tuesday's meeting will be brought into the process [3].\\n...\\nThe administration must also deliver on two other mandated deliverables from
the\\n...\\norder that were due by August 1: a\\n...\\nbenchmarking process involving the NSA\\n...\\nCISA,\\n...\\nNIST, and a\\n...\\ncyber workforce expansion plan from the Office of Personnel
Management. As of the deadline, it was unclear whether those had been completed [\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-04T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"White House Frontier AI

\"snippet\": \"White House Frontier AI Cybersecurity Framework Takes Shape, but Key Details Stay Secret -- Pure AI\\n\\nSkip to main content\\n\\nExpert Insights for the AI Business
Revolution\\n\\nAdd as a preferred source on Google\\n\\n### White House Frontier AI Cybersecurity Framework Takes Shape, but Key Details Stay Secret\\n\\nRepresentatives from leading artificial
intelligence developers met with White House officials Tuesday to review a voluntary framework for testing the cybersecurity capabilities and risks of advance\", \"highlights\": [\"Representatives
from leading artificial intelligence developers met with White House officials Tuesday to review a voluntary framework for testing the cybersecurity capabilities and risks of advanced models, but the
administration has not publicly disclosed the testing standards or what was decided.\\n...\\nStaffers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, and other AI companies were invited to the briefing.
No official announcement followed the meeting, and the details of the framework remain confidential.\\n...\\nThe framework would allow developers to provide the federal government with early access to
models that demonstrate advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Government agencies would then evaluate the models using a classified benchmarking process before they are made more widely
available.\\n...\\nUnder the order, developers can work with the government to determine whether a model qualifies as a \\u201ccovered frontier model.\\u201d Participating companies can provide
government evaluators with access for up to 30 days before the model is released to other trusted partners.\\n...\\nThe order requires confidentiality, cybersecurity, intellectual property, insider
risk\\n...\\nand nondisclosure protections for\\n...\\n. It also explicitly states that the program does not establish a mandatory licensing, pre\\n...\\nance, or permitting system for AI model
releases.\\n...\\nThe administration has not released the framework, identified the models likely to fall under it, or explained when testing will begin. The benchmark used to determine whether a
model has sufficiently advanced cyber capabilities is classified.\\n...\\nWhat Emerged After the Meeting No participant has publicly described a final agreement from Tuesday\\u2019s meeting. However,
according to reporting by Politico, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google had previously reviewed a draft version of the framework and submitted joint feedback to the White House roughly nine days prior. The
companies reportedly advocated that developers should be allowed to continue conducting A/B testing during model development without government interference, a position the White House
accepted.\\n...\\nAlthough the administration has not publicly confirmed specific conditions regarding federal funding or procurement leverage, the Office of Science and Technology Policy is actively
working on testing standards. The White House is also finalizing the roles that agencies such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security
Agency will play in evaluating these models.\\n...\\nAnother major limitation also became clearer after the meeting. The framework reportedly applies to proprietary models with state-of-the-art
cybersecurity capabilities but excludes open models, according to reports. That distinction could become increasingly difficult to defend if open models approach the cybersecurity capabilities of
closed frontier systems. A model\\u2019s risk does not disappear because its weights are downloadable. Open availability can make evaluation easier, but it can also make a capable model harder to
control after release.\\n...\\nVoluntary, But Not Without Leverage The framework is voluntary in a legal sense. It does not give the government general authority to approve or block model
releases.\\n...\\nLawmakers Press for More Transparency A group of Democratic senators raised concerns about that uncertainty in an August 3\\n...\\nto senior administration officials.\\n...\\nSens.
Kirsten Gillibrand, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Christopher Coons, and Mark Kelly called for a public, technically grounded framework and requested an unclassified response, with a classified annex, if
necessary, within 30 days.\\n...\\nThe senators asked the administration to explain how models will be classified as national security risks, which agencies will make those decisions, whether
independent experts will participate, and what appeal or remediation process will be available to developers.\\n...\\nthe White House has created\\n...\\nprocess that could shape access\\n...\\n. It
has not yet given the public enough information to judge how that process will work.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-05T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"White House Frontier-AI
Framework Done but Unpublished\", \"url\": \"https://agenccy.ai/news/white-house-frontier-model-framework-complete-unpublished/\", \"snippet\": \"White House Frontier-AI Framework Done but
Unpublished\\n\\n# The White House Says Its Frontier-Model Framework Is Finished. It Has Not Published It.\\n\\nExecutive Order 14409 gave the administration 60 days to design a voluntary framework
for evaluating advanced models. The deadline was 1 August. The announcement came on 3 August, and the document itself remains unreleased.\\n\\nAug 4, 2026Source: CNBC\\n\\nThe White House said on 3
August that the framework required by Executive Order 14409 is complete: \\\"The\", \"highlights\": [\"White House Frontier-AI Framework Done but Unpublished\\n\\n# The White House Says Its Frontier-
Model Framework Is Finished. It Has Not Published It.\\n\\nExecutive Order 14409 gave the administration 60 days to design a voluntary framework for evaluating advanced models. The deadline was 1
August. The announcement came on 3 August, and the document itself remains unreleased.\\n\\nAug 4, 2026Source: CNBC\\n\\nThe White House said on 3 August that the framework required by Executive Order
14409 is complete: \\\"The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order is complete. Discussions with industry about next steps are underway.\\\" A closed-door meeting with developers
followed on 4 August.\\n\\n## What the order actually requires\\n\\nEO 14409 was signed 2 June 2026 and published in the Federal Register on 5 June. It directs the design of \\\"a voluntary framework
with AI developers through which developers would be able to\\u2026 engage the Federal Government to determine whether model(s) under development meet the designation of 'covered frontier model.'\\\"
The 60-day clock ran to 1 August.\\n\\n## Voluntary means voluntary\\n\\nThis is not a rule and not a statute. A developer decides whether to seek a determination at all, and nothing in the order
compels participation. Representative Ted Lieu called the framework \\\"COMPLETELY VOLUNTARY\\\" and said companies are free to ignore it; Greg Casar and Pat Ryan objected to the voluntary approach as
such.\\n\\n## Announced is not published\\n\\nThe distinction that matters here is between a statement and a document. No text has been released, no evaluation criteria are public, and the threshold
for \\\"covered frontier model\\\" is unknown outside the meeting. There is also a timing dispute worth flagging as a dispute: the administration says it met the deadline, which fell two days before
the announcement.\\n\\n## Who owns it\\n\\nThe order hands the work to the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of War acting through the director of the NSA, and the Secretary of Homeland
Security acting through the director of CISA \\u2014 not to NIST or the science office, as much of the coverage assumes. It is a national-security assignment rather than a standards-body one, which
shapes what \\\"evaluation\\\" is likely to mean in practice. Staff from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta were called to the 4 August meeting.\\n\\n## Why It Matters\\n\\nThis is the federal
government's central mechanism for overseeing frontier models, and it has turned out to be voluntary and unpublished \\u2014 which shapes every argument about whether state AI laws are preempted or
necessary.\\n\\n## Related Stories\\n\\nChatGPT Will Now Log Your Clicks and Keystrokes to a File OpenAI Says Is Not Encrypted\\n\\n1d ago \\u00b7 AI Safety\\n\\nA Federal Judge Refused to Call an AI
Notetaker a Party to the Call\\n\\n1d ago \\u00b7 US AI Regulation\\n\\nAnthropic Put Claude Agents in a Shared Sandbox. They Wrote Malware at Each Other.\\n\\n1d ago \\u00b7 AI Safety\\n\\nA German
NGO Filed a Criminal Complaint Over Meta's Smart Glasses \\u2014 and Named the Shops Selling Them\\n\\n2d ago \\u00b7 AI Regulation\\n\\nEight AI Sub-Agents Ran 12 Attack Waves Against Taiwan's
Government. It Took Four Days.\\n\\n2d ago \\u00b7 AI Safety\\n\\nNorth Korean Operators Installed Their Own LLMs. That Is the Point.\\n\\n3d ago \\u00b7 AI Safety\"], \"published_date\":

your-customer\", \"snippet\": \"\\u2018Voluntary\\u2019 Until the Government Is Your Customer | Lawfare\\n\\nMeet The Authors\\n\\nThe new executive order on artificial intelligence (AI),

[\"The new executive\\n...\\non artificial intelligence (AI), \\u201cPromoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,\\u201d goes out of its way to say that its\\n...\\n-model
evaluation framework is voluntary. Section 3 of the framework directs agencies to design a process through which AI developers may engage with the government before releasing covered frontier models
to other trusted partners. The section then adds an explicit caveat: Nothing in\\n...\\n, preclearance, or permitting regime for developing, publishing, releasing, or distributing new\\n...\\nThe
order directs officials to develop a classified benchmarking process to determine when a model should be designated a \\u201ccovered frontier model.\\u201d It also calls for a voluntary framework:
Developers may seek that determination, give the government access for up to 30 days before a model is released to other trusted partners, and help choose the trusted partners whose early access is
intended to strengthen critical-infrastructure cybersecurity. Under the order, the director of the National Security Agency (NSA), in consultation with specified national security and cybersecurity
officials, determines whether to designate a frontier model as \\u201ccovered.\\u201d The designation authority is vested in the national security establishment, not in the civilian standards office
that has run the government\\u2019s frontier-model evaluation to date.\\n...\\nWithin days of the order\\u2019s signing, OpenAI said it would comply and give the government early access to its covered
frontier models. Sam Altman posted that the order \\u201cgets the balance right.\\u201d Anthropic called it \\u201can important step in strengthening America\\u2019s leadership in AI.\\u201d Which
raises the question: Why would companies embrace an order that cannot compel them?\\n...\\nThe order did not create government access to frontier models\\n...\\nSince 2024, the Commerce
Department\\u2019s Center for AI Standards and Innovation(CAISI), a National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) office, and its predecessor, the U.S. AI Safety Institute, have operated under
publicly announced agreements with OpenAI and Anthropic to evaluate their models before and after release. On May 5, the Commerce Department announced that Google, Microsoft, and xAI had joined, that
the original agreements had been renegotiated to align with the administration\\u2019s AI Action Plan, and that CAISI would serve as the industry\\u2019s primary point of contact within the government
for AI testing. CAISI also reported having completed more than 40 such assessments, including on models not yet released. The press release told the world, nearly four weeks before the executive
order, that a voluntary, centralized, civilian evaluation function was operating with the leading closed-model frontier developers inside it. In the wake of the order, however, that channel may have
narrowed: A week after the order was signed, the Wall Street Journal reported that administration officials had directed CAISI to halt public reporting on its model assessments while the executive
order is implemented. Testing continues internally, but the public-facing function is on hold.\\n...\\nEven as the civilian channel\\u2019s public work pauses, the signed order builds on that access
model and adds a decisive function the civilian program never had. The classified benchmarking process will determine which models count as covered frontier models. NIST is consulted in developing
that process, but the NSA director makes the designation itself. The existing evaluation relationships reside at the Commerce Department, in public agreements, inside a standards agency. The covered
designation will be made behind a classified benchmark, against an undisclosed threshold, on a basis no one outside the process can see.\\n...\\nis that each\\n...\\non a black-\\n...\\nprocess that
the public cannot see.\\n...\\nnominally voluntary.\\n...\\nthreshold\\u2014determined\\n...\\nexecutive-branch process\\u2014and\\n...\\nbecome the practical gatekeeper\\n...\\nthe federal
frontier\\n...\\nThe voluntary framework allows a developer to engage the government to determine whether a model under development meets the threshold, but nothing in the order conditions the NSA
director\\u2019s determination on a developer\\u2019s request. Assessments are shared with developers and researchers \\u201cas appropriate,\\u201d a case-by-case exercise of discretion that no firm
can demand as of right. Section 5(c) adds the common executive\\n...\\ndisclaimer: The order creates no right or benefit enforceable at law or in equity. The result is discretion on the way in, no
guaranteed process during, and no remedy under the order on the way out.\\n...\\nreach the visible solicitation terms, evaluations, or exclusions, but not necessarily the underlying classified
benchmark. Procurement can turn the designation\\n...\\nbefore any forum gets a\\n...\\nlook at the standard doing\\n...\\nThe window for getting this right is short, and the life cycle is the reason.
FedRAMP hardened around a public-facing baseline and authorization process. If this framework hardens, it will harden around a classified one. The order\\u2019s AI cybersecurity clearinghouse must be
established by July 2; the benchmarking process and voluntary framework are due by Aug. 1.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-06-23T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"White House Advances

3\\u20134, a dozen labs met the White House to 'close the loop' on a voluntary framework for frontier models. If you build on models instead of training them, it doesn't touch you directly. The Gold
Eagle clearinghouse is the part that reaches down to \", \"highlights\": [\"On August 3\\u20134, a dozen labs met the White House to 'close the loop' on a voluntary framework for frontier models. If
you build on models instead of training them, it doesn't touch you directly. The Gold Eagle clearinghouse is the part that reaches down to your stack.\\n...\\n- It stems from a June 2026 executive
order (EO 14409, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security'). The core mechanism: developers of 'covered frontier models' are invited \\u2014 voluntarily \\u2014 to give the
government up to 30 days of pre-release access for cybersecurity testing, down from a 90-day draft.\\n...\\n- 'Covered frontier model' is determined by a classified benchmarking process run by the NSA
(with CISA) that flags models with advanced cyber capabilities. By design it targets the largest labs' models, and it explicitly cannot be used to create mandatory licensing or pre-
clearance.\\n...\\nQuestion | The\\n...\\n|\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| Is it mandatory? | No \\u2014 voluntary participation for covered frontier models; cannot create licensing or pre-clearance | You
have no filing to make\\n...\\nno license to obtain |\\n...\\n| Who is 'covered'? | Models flagged by a classified NSA/CISA benchmark for advanced cyber capabilities | If you fine-tune or build on
existing models, you are almost certainly not covered |\\n...\\nthan the lab intended\\n...\\nOn August 3\\u20134, 2026, representatives from roughly a dozen AI companies \\u2014 including OpenAI,
Anthropic, Google, and Meta \\u2014 met White House officials to \\\"close the loop\\\" on a voluntary framework governing how frontier models reach the market (CNBC, Bloomberg). The meeting was short
\\u2014 reportedly about 30 minutes \\u2014 because the substance had already been negotiated over the prior two months.\\n...\\nThe framework traces back to a June 2026 executive order (EO 14409,
\\\"Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security\\\"). Its core mechanism is narrow: developers of a \\\"covered frontier model\\\" are invited \\u2014 voluntarily \\u2014 to
give federal agencies up to 30 days of pre-release access to test the model for cybersecurity risk. An earlier draft floated 90 days; the finalized version cut it to 30 to avoid handing China a speed
advantage (SiliconANGLE).\\n...\\nTwo design choices matter for how far this reaches. First, \\\"covered\\\" is decided by a classified benchmarking process run by the Director of the NSA, with CISA,
that flags models for advanced cyber capabilities \\u2014 a bar aimed squarely at frontier-scale systems, not fine-tuned or wrapped models. Second, the order says the framework cannot be used to
create mandatory licensing or pre-clearance. It is a testing invitation, not a gate you have to pass.\\n...\\nRead those two facts together and the founder answer is simple. If your company builds on
existing models \\u2014 you call an API, you fine-tune an open-weight model, you wrap a frontier model in a product \\u2014 you are not training a covered frontier model, and the classified benchmark
