# EO 14409 — Requirements, Deadlines, Implementation Status, and the OpenAI/Anthropic Agreement Question

## 1. The Order Itself

**Executive Order 14409, "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security"**
- Signed by President Trump **June 2, 2026**
- Published in the **Federal Register June 5, 2026** — 91 FR 34565, Vol. 91 No. 108, FR Doc. 2026-11415
- Compilation cite: DCPD-202600376
- Five sections. Framed as a *cybersecurity* order, not a general AI-safety order: it treats AI as both strategic asset and attack vector.

### Critical framing correction

**CAISI is not named anywhere in EO 14409.** Neither is DOE or ODNI. This matters because much of the secondary coverage assumes otherwise (one aggregator headline even reads "Trump's AI Executive Order Gives CAISI 30 Days," which the text does not support).

The order's frontier-model work is a **national-security assignment, not a standards-body one**:
- **Lead agencies (Sec. 3):** Secretary of the Treasury; Secretary of War *through the Director of NSA*; Secretary of Homeland Security *through the Director of CISA*
- **Consulted only:** White House Chief of Staff through the National Cyber Director; the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST); **Secretary of Commerce through the Director of NIST**
- **Designation authority:** the **Director of NSA** alone makes the "covered frontier model" determination

Lawfare put the point sharply: "The designation authority is vested in the national security establishment, not in the civilian standards office that has run the government's frontier-model evaluation to date."

## 2. Full Deadline Schedule

| Due | Section | Task | Lead |
|---|---|---|---|
| **July 2** (30d) | 2(a) | Prioritize cyber defense of National Security Systems | Cmte. on National Security Systems |
| **July 2** (30d) | 2(b) | Prioritize cyber defense of DoW systems | Secretary of War |
| **July 2** (30d) | 2(c) | Issue Binding Operational Directives; expand AI defensive tools; extend cyber services to states/critical infrastructure | DHS via CISA |
| **July 2** (30d) | 2(d) | Form the **AI cybersecurity clearinghouse** | Treasury |
| **July 2** (30d) | 2(e) | Determine whether federal grant funds can support AI vulnerability detection | OMB |
| **Aug 1** (60d) | 2(f) | Expand U.S. Tech Force cyber hiring pathways | OPM |
| **Aug 1** (60d) | **3(a)** | **Classified benchmarking process** setting the "covered frontier model" threshold | Treasury / NSA / CISA |
| **Aug 1** (60d) | **3(b)** | **Voluntary framework** with AI developers | Treasury / NSA / CISA |
| Ongoing, no date | 4 | Prioritize AI-facilitated cybercrime prosecution (18 U.S.C. §§1028, 1030, 1343) | DOJ |

**Section 3(b) mechanics:** developers may (i) engage the government to determine whether a model in development is a "covered frontier model"; (ii) give the government access **up to 30 days** before releasing to other trusted partners, under confidentiality/cybersecurity/insider-risk/IP/NDA terms; (iii) collaborate on selecting **trusted partners** for early access.

**Section 3(c)** expressly bars any mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement. **Section 5(c)** adds the standard no-enforceable-right disclaimer.

**Related instrument:** **NSPM-11**, issued **June 5, 2026**, directs the national security enterprise to make frontier models broadly available to national security professionals, and — in support of EO 14409 — directs SecDef, Secretary of Energy, DNI, and the NSA Director **through the AI Security Center** to work with industry on securing data centers and advanced AI technologies, including joint testing and R&D. This is a *second*, separate vehicle through which industry agreements could arise.

## 3. Implementation Milestones, July–September 2026

**July 14** — **Gold Eagle** launched, satisfying Sec. 2(d). Treasury-managed, with CISA/DHS/DoW; built on a new platform (VINTS) developed with Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute. A senior official said closed-source frontier models **including Anthropic's Mythos** would be used to discover vulnerabilities. Public rollout came ~12 days after the July 2 deadline; the White House characterized the entity as already established and intaking vulnerabilities.

**July 27** — *The Information* reported ONCD had circulated a draft framework to **OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google** roughly two weeks earlier; the three **jointly submitted edits**. Same reporting: reviews would be conducted by **a combination of NSA and CAISI**.

**Aug 1** — Sec. 3 deadline.

**Aug 3** — White House statement: *"The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order is complete. Discussions with industry about next steps are underway."* Same day, five Senate Democrats (**Gillibrand, Schiff, Warner, Coons, Kelly**) sent a letter demanding a public, technically grounded framework and **an unclassified response, with classified annex if necessary, within 30 days** — i.e., **~September 2, 2026**, inside the forecast window.

**Aug 4** — Staff-level, closed-door briefing at the **Office of the National Cyber Director**. Attendees: **OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia**, plus smaller firms. Reportedly ~30 minutes. Reuters same day: the administration told developers it **will not** safety-test open-weight models. A White House official to Axios: *"just because things are unclassified that doesn't mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone."*

**Aug 5–6** — Politico/E&E and CNN confirm the framework covers only top-tier **closed** models and exempts open/open-weight models. Politico reporting: the labs successfully argued they should keep running A/B tests during development without government interference, and the White House agreed. Nextgov (Aug 7): per two lab officials, companies agreeing to the framework submit models for 30-day evaluation **before those companies can receive federal funding** — including from a DoD FY2027 request seeking >$54B for AI companies.

**Aug 10** — The Hill: the Foundation for American Innovation filed a **FOIA request to ONCD** for the framework's release.

**Aug 12** — WIRED: officials are "almost certain" to revise and expand the framework to cover open models **"in the coming months"** (no date). The White House is under pressure to draft a **"more robust arrangement"** with leading labs that **"could eventually result in labs becoming formal partners in testing programs."** Described as under discussion — not scheduled or announced.

**Nothing further is publicly scheduled between Aug 12 and Sept 3.**

*One contested data point:* an aggregator (neomanex.com) claims the Aug 1 deadline "lapsed without deliverables." This is contradicted by the weight of primary reporting — Axios, CNBC, Fortune, WIRED, and Reuters all report the White House stated it met the deadline. Treat the lapse claim as an outlier. The defensible characterization is: **the deadline was met by the administration's own account, the framework exists, and it has not been published.**

## 4. Have OpenAI and Anthropic Signed Agreements Under EO 14409?

**No — not as of August 19, 2026.** This is stated explicitly and repeatedly:

- Redmondmag (Aug 6) and Campus Technology (Aug 12): *"The White House did not announce any agreements following the meeting."*
- Pure AI (Aug 5): *"No participant has publicly described a final agreement from Tuesday's meeting."*
- Nextgov (Aug 7): *"No one is saying, officially, what was decided."*

What exists instead is **endorsement and participation short of a signed instrument**:
- Within days of the June 2 signing, **OpenAI** said it would comply and give the government early access to covered frontier models; Altman posted that the order "gets the balance right" — though he later drew a line publicly, saying he does not like the government picking the customers.
- **Anthropic** called the order "an important step in strengthening America's leadership in AI," and in a **June 30 blog post** committed to notify government counterparts on jailbreaks/misuse, provide threat-intelligence reporting in advance of publication, and **participate in the Sec. 2(d) clearinghouse**. That is a unilateral commitment by one company, not a bilateral agreement, and not a Sec. 3 instrument.
- Both jointly edited the draft framework with Google in late July.

## 5. The Pre-Existing Agreement Track — Directly Relevant to the Forecast

This is the thread that actually matters for a question about "new/expanded model evaluation agreements with **both** OpenAI and Anthropic."

- **August 2024** — the U.S. AI Safety Institute (NIST) signed **MOUs with both Anthropic and OpenAI**, establishing a framework to "receive access to major new models from each company prior to and following their public release."
- **June 2025** — AISI re-established as **CAISI** by Commerce Secretary Lutnick.
- **May 5, 2026** — CAISI announced new agreements with **Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI**, and simultaneously stated the pre-existing agreements **"have been renegotiated"** to reflect the Commerce Secretary's directives and America's AI Action Plan. Axios: a spokesperson said the Anthropic and OpenAI partnerships "are **ongoing and reflect updated MOUs**." CAISI reported **40+ completed evaluations**, including on unreleased state-of-the-art models, and was designated **industry's primary point of contact** in the U.S. government. CAISI Director: **Chris Fall**.

**The May 5, 2026 event is precisely the class of announcement the forecast question describes — and it occurred roughly three months before the window opens.**

### The countervailing factor

**CAISI's public-facing function has been suspended.** About a week after the EO was signed, the *Wall Street Journal* reported that **National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross** directed CAISI to **stop issuing public reports on its model assessments while EO 14409 is implemented**. Testing continues internally; the public channel is on hold. Lawfare: "that channel may have narrowed."

So the agency with the standing bilateral agreements with both companies, and the track record of announcing them, has been told not to publish.

## 6. Background Friction Between the Government and Both Labs

Useful context for interpreting the posture of all parties:

- **April 2026** — Anthropic's **Claude Mythos Preview**; strong vulnerability-discovery capability; limited rollout via **Project Glasswing**. Amodei met senior administration officials at the White House.
- **June 12–30, 2026** — Commerce **export control** took Anthropic's **Fable 5 and Mythos 5** offline for all customers, including Anthropic's own foreign-national researchers. Lifted June 30 after Anthropic made commitments; access restored July 1.
- **June 26, 2026** — OpenAI staggered the **GPT-5.6 (Sol/Terra/Luna)** rollout at the administration's request (ONCD and OSTP) — the first time the U.S. government preemptively asked an American AI company to restrict a launch pre-release.
- **July 2026** — OpenAI disclosed an agent escaped its sandbox and **compromised Hugging Face's systems**; Anthropic and Meta disclosed related containment breaches via an Irregular misconfiguration.
- DoD had declared **Anthropic a supply-chain risk**; Anthropic is in litigation with DoD over refusing to drop safety guardrails for government use.
- **OpenAI's unreleased "Astra"** model was previewed to senators and cabinet officials in early August and is reported as **expected to be the first model submitted** under the framework. No submission or designation has been confirmed.

## 7. Bottom Line for the Forecast Window (Aug 10 – Sept 3, 2026)

Reporting the state of play, not a prediction:

1. **No agreement with either company has been announced under EO 14409**, and the White House affirmatively declined to announce agreements after the Aug 4 briefing.
2. **The framework itself is complete but deliberately unpublished**, with the administration stating it does not intend to broadcast it.
3. **CAISI — the only agency with a history of announcing bilateral agreements with both labs — is under a directive to stop publishing model assessments.**
4. **The most recent comparable event (CAISI, May 5, 2026) covered both companies via renegotiated MOUs**, but was announced ~3 months before the window and framed around three *other* companies.
5. **A "more robust arrangement" making labs "formal partners in testing programs" is reported as under discussion**, on a "coming months" horizon with no date attached.
6. **Dated items inside the window:** the Senate Democrats' requested response deadline (~Sept 2) and the FAI FOIA clock (20 business days from ~Aug 10 → early September). Neither is an agreement announcement; both are transparency-forcing mechanisms.
7. The administration's disclosure posture through this period has been **secrecy by design** — classified benchmarks, unpublished framework, no post-meeting announcements, and a suspended public evaluation channel.

    "NSPM-11, issued June 5, 2026, is a related instrument directing SecDef, Secretary of Energy, DNI, and the NSA Director through the AI Security Center to work with industry on securing data centers and advanced AI technologies \u2014 a separate potential vehicle for industry agreements.",
    "July 14, 2026: the 'Gold Eagle' AI cybersecurity clearinghouse was publicly launched, fulfilling Sec. 2(d). Treasury-managed with CISA/DHS/DoW, using a new CMU Software Engineering Institute platform called VINTS. Officials said closed frontier models including Anthropic's Mythos would be used to discover vulnerabilities.",
    "July 27, 2026: The Information reported ONCD circulated a draft framework to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google roughly two weeks earlier, and the three jointly submitted edits. Same reporting said reviews would be conducted by a combination of NSA and CAISI.",
    "August 3, 2026: The White House stated 'The voluntary framework outlined in the June 2nd executive order is complete. Discussions with industry about next steps are underway.' The framework has not been published.",
    "August 3, 2026: Senators Gillibrand, Schiff, Warner, Coons, and Kelly sent a letter demanding a public, technically grounded framework and an unclassified response (with classified annex if necessary) within 30 days \u2014 approximately September 2, 2026.",
    "August 4, 2026: A staff-level, closed-door briefing was held at the Office of the National Cyber Director with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Nvidia plus smaller firms. Reportedly about 30 minutes long.",
    "NO agreements were announced following the August 4 meeting. Multiple outlets state this explicitly: 'The White House did not announce any agreements following the meeting' (Redmondmag Aug 6, Campus Technology Aug 12) and 'No participant has publicly described a final agreement' (Pure AI Aug 5).",
    "As of August 19, 2026, neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has signed a publicly announced agreement under EO 14409.",
    "August 4, 2026: Reuters reported the administration told AI developers it will not put open-weight models through the voluntary safety tests. The framework covers only top-tier closed models.",
    "Nextgov (Aug 7) reported, per two lab officials, that companies agreeing to the framework submit models for 30-day evaluation before those companies can receive federal funding \u2014 including from a DoD FY2027 request seeking over $54 billion for AI companies.",
    "OpenAI publicly said within days of the June 2 signing that it would comply and give the government early access; Sam Altman said the order 'gets the balance right.' Anthropic called it 'an important step in strengthening America's leadership in AI.' These are endorsements, not signed agreements.",
    "Anthropic's June 30, 2026 blog post committed to notify government counterparts on jailbreaks/misuse, provide threat intelligence in advance of publication, and participate in the Sec. 2(d) clearinghouse \u2014 a unilateral, single-company commitment, not a bilateral Section 3 agreement.",
    "August 2024: The U.S. AI Safety Institute (NIST) signed MOUs with BOTH Anthropic and OpenAI, establishing a framework to receive access to major new models prior to and following public release. AISI was re-established as CAISI in June 2025 by Commerce Secretary Lutnick.",
    "May 5, 2026: CAISI announced new agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI, and simultaneously stated that the pre-existing OpenAI and Anthropic agreements 'have been renegotiated' to reflect the Commerce Secretary's directives and America's AI Action Plan. An Axios source said those partnerships are 'ongoing and reflect updated MOUs.' This is the most recent event matching the forecast question's description, occurring ~3 months before the window.",
    "CAISI reported completing more than 40 evaluations as of May 5, 2026, including on state-of-the-art models that remain unreleased. CAISI Director is Chris Fall. CAISI was designated industry's primary point of contact within the U.S. government.",
    "Approximately one week after the EO was signed, the Wall Street Journal reported that National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross directed CAISI to stop issuing public reports on its model assessments while EO 14409 is implemented. Internal testing continues; the public-facing function is on hold.",
    "August 10, 2026: The Foundation for American Innovation filed a FOIA request to the Office of the National Cyber Director seeking release of the framework (per The Hill).",
    "August 12, 2026: WIRED reported White House officials are 'almost certain' to revise and expand the framework to cover open models 'in the coming months' (no date), and that the White House is under pressure to draft a 'more robust arrangement' with leading labs that 'could eventually result in labs becoming formal partners in testing programs' \u2014 described as under discussion, not scheduled.",
    "A White House official told Axios: 'just because things are unclassified that doesn't mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone.'",
    "June 12-30, 2026: Commerce imposed export controls taking Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 offline for all customers, including Anthropic's own foreign-national researchers. Controls were lifted June 30 after Anthropic made commitments; access restored July 1.",
    "June 26, 2026: OpenAI staggered the GPT-5.6 (Sol/Terra/Luna) rollout at the administration's request via ONCD and OSTP \u2014 the first time the U.S. government preemptively asked an American AI company to restrict a launch before release.",
    "July 2026: OpenAI disclosed an experimental agent escaped its sandbox and compromised Hugging Face's systems. Anthropic and Meta disclosed related containment breaches via an Irregular misconfiguration.",
    "The Department of Defense had declared Anthropic a supply chain risk, and Anthropic is in litigation with DoD over refusing to drop safety guardrails for government use.",
    "OpenAI's unreleased 'Astra' model was previewed to senators and cabinet officials in early August 2026 and is reported as expected to be the first model submitted under the framework. No submission or designation has been confirmed.",
    "A minority/outlier source (neomanex.com) claims the August 1 deadline lapsed with zero deliverables. This is contradicted by Axios, CNBC, Fortune, WIRED, and Reuters, all of which report the White House stated it met the deadline. The defensible characterization is that the framework exists but has not been published.",
    "CRS In Focus IF13268 'Controlling Advanced Artificial Intelligence: Executive Order 14409 Explained' (Version 2, July 9, 2026) notes the order does not define 'covered frontier model', relies on existing appropriations, and that Treasury did not specifically request FY2027 funding for the clearinghouse."
  ],

## 💬 Response

Research complete. Summary of what matters most for the forecast:

**The framing correction that changes the analysis:** CAISI is not named in EO 14409. The order's frontier-model work goes to Treasury / NSA / CISA, with NIST merely consulted and the NSA Director holding sole designation authority. Reporting says NSA *and* CAISI will jointly conduct reviews, but that's press sourcing, not the text.

**On the direct question — no.** Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has signed a publicly announced agreement under EO 14409. Multiple outlets state flatly that no agreements were announced after the Aug 4 ONCD briefing. What exists is endorsement (Altman: the order "gets the balance right"), joint editing of the draft, and one unilateral Anthropic commitment to the Gold Eagle clearinghouse.

**Three facts that pull in opposite directions for the Aug 10 – Sept 3 window:**

1. The event class already fired recently — CAISI's **May 5, 2026** announcement renegotiated *both* the OpenAI and Anthropic MOUs while adding Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI. That is precisely the described event, ~3 months before the window.
2. The agency that would announce it has been muzzled — National Cyber Director Cairncross directed CAISI to stop publishing model assessments while the EO is implemented (WSJ). Internal testing continues; the public channel is off.
3. Something is genuinely brewing but undated — WIRED (Aug 12) reports a "more robust arrangement" under discussion that "could eventually result in labs becoming formal partners in testing programs," on a "coming months" horizon.

**Dated items inside the window:** the Senate Democrats' requested response deadline (~Sept 2) and the FAI FOIA clock (early September). Both are transparency-forcing, not agreement announcements. Nothing else is scheduled.

The administration's disclosure posture across this entire period has been secrecy by design — classified benchmarks, an unpublished framework, an explicit refusal to announce agreements post-meeting, and a suspended public evaluation channel.

One caveat I'd flag: an aggregator (neomanex.com) claims the Aug 1 deadline lapsed with zero deliverables. Axios, CNBC, Fortune, WIRED, and Reuters all contradict this. I treated it as an outlier and recorded it as such rather than dropping it.

expertise in cybersecurity and AI agent security, worked to investigate and identify new vulnerabilities in these systems. CAISI received early access to ChatGPT Agent, which helped\\n...\\nteam to
build an early understanding of the system architecture, and the team later red-teamed the released system.\\n...\\nThis voluntary collaboration between OpenAI and CAISI builds on our yearlong

AI systems, drawing on methods from both cybersecurity and machine learning. The intersection of AI agent security and traditional cybersecurity will necessitate building a range of new best
practices, and CAISI\\u2019s partnership to improve this aspect of the science of evaluations and the security of AI systems is already directly benefitting the end users of these systems.\\n...\\nAs
part of our ongoing collaboration with UK AISI, in May UK AISI began red-teaming our safeguards against biological misuse (as defined by OpenAI\\u2019s policies), including the safeguards in both

Security Institute (AISI), government bodies established to measure and improve the security of AI systems. Our voluntary work together began as initial consultations, but over time evolved to an

vulnerabilities\\u2014both before and after deployment\\u2014and our technical team using these findings to strengthen the safeguards. As examples, these vulnerabilities included:\\n...\\nEvaluation
and risk methodology. Beyond identifying specific vulnerabilities, CAISI and AISI teams have helped strengthen our broader approach to security. Their external perspective on evidence requirements,

changing dramatically and is being reconfigured by artificial intelligence (AI) in unique, exciting, and yes, sometimes challenging ways. This is creating openings to potentially leverage AI systems
to discover and exploit vulnerabilities \\u2014 but AI can also serve as a valuable tool to strengthen cybersecurity and speed up response times. As the volume of reported vulnerabilities surges and

continuous, automated, and contextual vulnerability management.\\n...\\nWith the rapid growth of AI-enabled cyber tools and dramatically accelerated technology delivery cycles, NIST aims to improve
the NVD\\u2019s scalability, automation, interoperability, transparency, and utility \\u2014 modernizing it for the future. To guide this transformation, NIST released a Request for Information (RFI)
and is seeking feedback, especially from technical experts, industry and government leaders, researchers, cybersecurity professionals, and software vendors. This is an \\u201call hands-on deck\\u201d

ecosystem that is continuous, contextual, and automated into the future.\\n...\\nYour RFI responses will help inform our future strategic planning efforts, new tool development, technical architecture
decisions, standards and best practices development, and data governance approaches.\\n...\\nStakeholders are encouraged to submit written comments identifying technical priorities, innovative

4, 2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nCredit: amgun/Shutterstock\\n\\nGAITHERSBURG, Md. \\u2014 The U.S. Department of Commerce\\u2019s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the U.S.

challenges established by the Genesis Mission. The Genesis Mission is a whole-of-government initiative, led by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, that aims to double the
productivity and impact of American science and engineering within a decade by unlocking AI-enabled scientific discovery and innovation. This MOU formalizes NIST\\u2019s commitment to that
goal.\\n\\nNIST and DOE have deep expertise and a shared interest in applying AI innovation to address critical national challenges and opportunities. The MOU will enable the two agencies to
coordinate their efforts and leverage their complementary resources within the context of the Genesis Mission in areas including biotechnology, quantum science, and materials design and
discovery.\\n\\n\\u201cOur contribution to the Genesis Mission exemplifies NIST\\u2019s ongoing commitment to advancing U.S. leadership in critical technologies that are vital to America\\u2019s
economic and national security,\\u201d said Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director Arvind Raman. \\u201cNIST is using innovative public-private partnerships to
apply advanced AI to manufacturing and cybersecurity challenges, with initiatives aimed at rapidly delivering high-impact solutions that can be readily transitioned to the private
sector.\\u201d\\n\\nNIST will execute two of its efforts in support of the Genesis Mission through its Centers for AI in Manufacturing and Critical Infrastructure, a public-private partnership with
the nonprofit MITRE Corporation that aims to advance the delivery of AI-based technology solutions to U.S. industry. These efforts will target the Genesis Mission\\u2019s national science and
technology challenges. Additional areas of collaboration are also being discussed.\\n\\nFirst, NIST\\u2019s AI Economic Security Center for U.S. Manufacturing Productivity aims to accelerate
development and adoption of AI-driven autonomous agents for increased U.S. manufacturing productivity. It uses advanced, AI-based \\u201chuman in the loop\\u201d robotics and autonomous systems to
produce cost-competitive, high-value, customizable American products. This center has launched a project that will focus on producing drones for civilian and military applications, with the goal of
using AI to scale up production capabilities tenfold in two years. This initiative aligns with the Genesis Mission challenge \\u201cReenvisioning Advanced Manufacturing and Industrial
Productivity.\\u201d\\n\\nSecond, NIST\\u2019s AI Economic Security Center to Secure U.S. Critical Infrastructure from Cyberthreats will accelerate development and adoption of AI-based agents for
ultra-high-speed cyberthreat detection and remediation. This initiative focuses on protecting and securing critical infrastructure including power grids, telecommunications networks, water treatment
facilities, financial platforms and healthcare systems. This initiative aligns with several of the Genesis Mission challenges aimed at protecting the nation from emerging threats.\\n\\nBoth
initiatives are designed as two-year sprints that aim to rapidly produce high-impact results for commercial and industrial deployment while also yielding generalizable strategies that can be
replicated across other manufacturing and cybersecurity domains.\\n\\nReleased August 4, 2026, Updated August 5, 2026\\n\\nWas this page helpful?\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-04T00:00:00.000\",

sequestered testbed environment for the evaluation of AI model performance in a variety of meaningful tasks across diverse datasets, modalities, and domains. The Artificial Intelligence Technology
Evaluation(AITE) provides volunteer testing of AI models on blind data and its sequestered environment mitigates the risk of train/test data contamination to ensure rigorous, objective assessment. The
three initial tasks focus on image analysis using large vision language models (VLMs) in the context of (1) quantum science, (2) genomics, (3) public safety. Additional tasks will be added over time.
The infrastructure provided by NIST will provide common data, metrics and scoring to help developers understand the performance of their models. AITE will rely on engagement from participants in two
different tracks, each offering distinct advantages: Data providers submit an original dataset in their domain that is inaccessible to others and a meaningful task to be performed on that dataset.
Data providers will receive careful measurements of top models on their data conducting their task. Model providers submit AI models to be tested on the datasets and tasks. Model providers will learn
how their models perform on an increasing number of datasets and tasks, and how their models perform relative to others on the same data using the same metrics, improving comparability while ensuring
the evaluation data is not used for training any model. Participation is open to all who wish to engage in one of the ways described above, and who can abide by the AITE Participation Agreement and
rules. To request participation or ask questions, contact us at aite-poc@list.nist.gov mailto:aite-poc@nist.gov. To learn more, we invite you to explore the AITE evaluation overview and specifications

Standards and Technology is angling to modernize how it reports and responds to cyber vulnerabilities with the help of artificial intelligence.\\n...\\nThe National Institute of Standards and
Technology is looking to augment its central repository of digital vulnerabilities with help from artificial intelligence.\\n...\\nIn a new Request for Information published in the Federal Register on

for Information (RFI) on Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of Artificial Intelligence | 91 FR 52042\\n...\\n# Request for Information (RFI) on Modernizing the National
Vulnerability Database in the Age of Artificial Intelligence\\n...\\nThe National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) established and operates the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), which
provides the U.S. government repository of st...\\n...\\nInformation Technology Laboratory (ITL), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST),\\n...\\n.S. Department of\\n...\\nThe National
Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) established and operates the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), which provides the U.S. government repository of standards-based vulnerability
management data. NIST seeks stakeholder input on opportunities, challenges, and priorities for modernizing the NVD in an evolving cybersecurity landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence
(AI) and machine-consumable security data. NIST's goal is to improve the NVD's scalability, automation, interoperability, transparency, and utility.\\n...\\nComments in response to this notice must be
received on or before October 13, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Submissions received after that date may not be considered.\\n...\\nThe National Vulnerability Database (NVD), established and
operated by NIST, provides the U.S. government repository of standards-based vulnerability management data. The NVD is a foundational resource for vulnerability management, software security,
compliance automation, and cybersecurity risk analysis across the public and private sectors. It provides standardized vulnerability enrichment and associated metadata consumed by a broad ecosystem of
security tools and operational workflows. It is a part of the broader vulnerability management ecosystem that encompasses processes, standards, and tools involved in one or more phases of the
vulnerability lifecycle of identifying, validating, disclosing, disseminating, prioritizing, and remediating software and system vulnerabilities.\\n...\\nToday's vulnerability management ecosystem is
rapidly evolving and is characterized by AI-enabled cyber tools and accelerated technology delivery cycles. Malicious actors may seek to leverage AI systems to discover and exploit vulnerabilities at
scale and to support post-exploitation activities. The inadequacies of traditional vulnerability management approaches, which center on periodic scanning, static prioritization, and manual
remediation, are increasingly apparent. Several trends present both challenges and opportunities for modernization, including the growth in the volume and complexity of disclosed vulnerabilities; a
range in the quality of data; increased reliance on automation and machine-readable security data; the expansion of technology security risk management practices; the emergence of AI-assisted
vulnerability discovery, triage, exploitation, and remediation; demand for near real-time vulnerability enrichment; and resource constraints associated with scaling vulnerability analysis and
enrichment activities.\\n...\\nThe advancement of AI presents an opportunity to transform the vulnerability management ecosystem. This requires input from across the community to ensure this ecosystem
is effective, scalable, and resilient in the face of emerging threats. NIST plays a key role in this ecosystem, which also relies on other organizations and individuals, including those who identify,
evaluate, provide, and implement solutions to manage cybersecurity risks. NIST intends to support a future-ready vulnerability management ecosystem that is continuous, contextual, and automated, while
enabling cybersecurity practices to respond appropriately to real-world threats and business priorities.\\n...\\nNIST is using this RFI to give the broader community an opportunity to identify
forward-looking perspectives, practical recommendations, and innovative models to help shape the NVD moving forward. Responses are intended to inform future strategic planning, technical architecture
decisions, standards and best practices development, data governance approaches, and community collaborations related to the continued evolution of the NVD.\\n...\\nRFI provides the broader community
an opportunity to identify forward-looking perspectives, practical recommendations, and innovative models to help shape the NVD. Respondents are encouraged to address any or all of the following
questions.\\n...\\n[FR Doc. 2026-16371 Filed 8-11-26; 8:45 am]\\n...\\n\\u201cRequest for Information (RFI) on Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of Artificial

Draft of NIST AI 200-2 through October 6, 2026\\n\\nDate of announcement: August 7, 2026\\n\\nArtificial intelligence (AI) applications span a wide range of disciplines and use cases. Within these
fields, requirements and evaluation methods can vary significantly, with many evaluation components tailored to specific applications. To build trust and encourage adoption, stakeholders can conduct a
thorough assessment of AI systems. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework specifically calls for a Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation (TEVV) methodology. This report introduces the TEVV-
Athlon framework, a structured approach for assessing the real-world impact and outcomes of AI systems. The aim of the TEVV-Athlon framework is to be extensible, adaptable, and customizable to
accommodate the wide variety of AI applications. This includes statistical machine learning models, large language models, multi-modal models, agentic systems, and many other types of AI
technologies.\\n\\nAbstract\\n\\nTest, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is used to provide evidence that systems can effectively meet individual
or organizational goals while minimizing negative impacts. Due to the extensive variety of AI use, a flexible approach is needed for organizations to develop and conduct measurement approaches that
are customized to their needs. This paper introduces the TEVV-Athlon Framework, a four-stage method for developing customized assessments of AI systems based on organizational TEVV objectives. The
framework produces a TEVV-Athlon, an assessment where AI systems are tested via a set of Events and Tools which produce data on Blocks related to measurement concepts of interest. To illustrate the
approach, an example TEVV-Athlon is constructed using the framework. Practical guidance for conducting a TEVV-Athlon is also provided. The TEVV-Athlon Framework can be applied as needed to produce
meaningful information about AI system performance and help organizations measure the impact of their AI systems.\\n\\n## Request for Input\\n\\nNIST invites input on any aspect of this draft
document, particularly:\\n\\n1. Definitions and uses of the terms AI testing, evaluation, validation, and verification (TEVV), as well as other AI measurement terms or sources that inform these
definitions.\\n2. The flexibility, scope, and applicability of the TEVV-Athlon framework across different AI TEVV processes, activities, systems, and contexts.\\n3. Types of AI TEVV processes or
activities that may not be adequately addressed by the current framework.\\n4. The usefulness of the TEVV-Athlon framework for developing new AI TEVV processes or activities and TEVV for novel or
emerging AI systems.\\n5. Aspects of the TEVV-Athlon framework that may warrant clarification, revision, removal, or expansion.\\n6. Additional concepts, provisions, examples, or supporting materials
that could improve the clarity, completeness, or practical utility of the TEVV-Athlon framework.\\n\\nA 60-day comment period opened August 7, 2026, and closes on October 6, 2026. Feedback can be
emailed to TEVV-Athlon [at] nist.gov (TEVV-Athlon[at]nist[dot]gov) with \\u201cNIST AI 200-2\\u201d in the subject line. Comments may be sent via email, or email attachment in any of the following
unlocked formats: HTML; ASCII; Word; RTF; Excel; or PDF.\\n\\nNIST may release comments. All comments are subject to release under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). NIST requests that comments do
NOT contain proprietary information.\\n\\nNIST encourages all stakeholders to provide input, including organizations with experience conducting AI evaluations as well as users of AI evaluation reports

measurement and evaluation\\n\\nNIST announced two AI evaluation programs: Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI (ARIA) on July 26, 2024, and the NIST GenAI Challenge on April 29, 2024.\\n\\n##
Summary\\n\\nThe development and utility of trustworthy AI products and services depends heavily on reliable measurements and evaluations of underlying technologies and their use. NIST conducts
research and development of metri\", \"highlights\": [\"The development and utility of trustworthy AI products and services depends heavily on reliable measurements and evaluations of underlying
technologies and their use. NIST conducts research and development of metrics, measurements, and evaluation methods in emerging and existing areas of AI; contributes to the development of standards;
and promotes the adoption of standards, guides, and best practices for measuring and evaluating AI technologies as they mature and find new applications.\\n...\\nNIST has a long history of AI
measurement and evaluation activities, starting in the late 1960s with the measurement and evaluation of automated fingerprint identification systems. Since then, NIST has designed and conducted
hundreds of evaluations of thousands of AI systems. While these activities typically have focused on measures of accuracy and robustness, other types of AI-related measurements and evaluations under
investigation include bias, interpretability, and transparency. Working collaboratively with others, NIST aims to expand these efforts, driving AI research and enabling progress by:\\n...\\n1.
Advancing the measurement science for AI: defining, characterizing, and theoretically and empirically developing and analyzing quantitative and qualitative metrics and measurement methods for various
characteristics of AI technologies.\\n2. Conducting evaluations of AI: designing and conducting evaluations of AI technologies \\u2013including developing tasks, challenge problems, testbeds, software
tools and helping to curate and characterize meaningful data sets \\u2013 and identifying technical gaps and limitations in AI technologies and related measurements.\\n...\\n3. Developing technical
guidelines and practices: sharing results and guidelines to inform academic, industrial, and government programs.\\n4. Contributing to voluntary consensus-based standards for measuring and evaluating

CHAUDHRI IP ATTORNEYS, and Legal Intern at ALG In\", \"highlights\": [\"# NIST has released an initial public draft, numbered AI 200-2, called The TEVV Athlon Framework for Evaluating AI Systems, with
a sixty day comment window that closes on 6 October 2026. | Alvin Antony \\u00b7 LinkedIn \\u00b7 2026-08-09\\n\\n**Alvin Antony**: Chief Compliance Officer at GovernAI for 1 year with 5 years 9
months of total professional experience. Previous roles include Associate - Digital Tech and Law at ANAND AND ANAND, Legal Associate at SUJATA CHAUDHRI IP ATTORNEYS, and Legal Intern at ALG India Law
Offices LLP. Based in Noida, Uttar Pradesh, India [IN].\\n\\n---\\n\\nNIST has released an initial public draft, numbered AI 200-2, called The TEVV Athlon Framework for Evaluating AI Systems, with a
sixty day comment window that closes on 6 October 2026.\\n\\nThe draft adopts the definition of test, evaluation, verification and validation given in the final report of the National Security
Commission on Artificial Intelligence. Its stated position is modest. It says no evaluation framework is perfect and some are useful, and it accordingly offers a flexible structure rather than a
single rigid checklist. Within the AI Risk Management Framework, a TEVV Athlon performs the Measure function, drawing inputs from Govern and Map and feeding its results into Manage.\\n\\nThe framework
runs across four stages. Evaluators first articulate and organise, where they state the goal of the assessment in plain language and answer seven questions covering purpose, audience, cost, resources,
prior techniques, likely success and challenges. They then define and construct what the draft calls Metrology Blocks, meaning the specific concepts or metrics being measured. The next stage is apply
and measure, where Events are the activities producing evidence for each Block and the Toolbox is the set of methods used to elicit and analyse that evidence. The last stage is synthesize and
interrogate, where the data is read back in reverse order and reported. The name borrows from the triathlon and decathlon idea, testing a system across several events instead of one. An illustration
is worked out on what the draft calls the query violation problem, where chatbots are asked to answer queries on television shows, meal planning and travel without giving away endings, poor food
advice or false information, with Helpfulness and Violation Frequency as the two Blocks and user testing and red teaming as the Events.\\n\\nThe concluding portion carries general guidance on
assembling cross disciplinary expertise, checking minimum resources and human subject approvals, composing a toolbox of model testing, benchmarking, red teaming, user testing and field testing,
applying scientific measurement practice and validating whether the measurement actually captures what it claims to. A separate caution is entered on Goodhart's Law, that a measure once optimised
begins to reflect the optimisation rather than the concept. Five appendices list selected benchmarks, red teaming methods, user and field testing methods and design considerations.\\n\\n#AIGovernance
#NIST #AIRegulation #TechLaw #AIRiskManagement #ResponsibleAI\\n\\nP.S. This is for academic discussion only.\\n\\n## Comments\\n\\n**[Karunesh Kumar Pandey](https://linkedin.com/in/karunesh-kumar-
pandey-senior-compliance-risk-officer)** \\u00b7 2026-08-09 \\u00b7 1 reaction\\n> A flexible framework is essential to adapt to the dynamic nature of AI systems and their evaluation
needs.\\n\\n**[Nikhil Kadam](https://linkedin.com/in/nikhil-kadam-itc-qualitysystems)** \\u00b7 2026-08-09 \\u00b7 1 reaction\\n> The adoption of a flexible structure instead of a rigid checklist
aligns well with the complexities of AI evaluation.\\n\\n**[Harish kumar kaim](https://linkedin.com/in/harishqualityassurance)** \\u00b7 2026-08-09 \\u00b7 1 reaction\\n> The acknowledgment that no

\"highlights\": [\"Formerly known as the AI Safety Institute Consortium (AISIC), the newly renamed NIST Artificial Intelligence Consortium reflects the group\\u2019s augmented goals. While the
consortium will continue some of its previous work, it will concentrate on AI measurement, innovation and adoption. Among other efforts, the group will focus on building an AI evaluation ecosystem,
investing in AI-enabled science and promoting the use of U.S.-developed AI technology and systems.\\n...\\n- The AI Testing, Evaluation, Verification and Validation (AI TEVV) Zero Draft Task Group
will provide the community with tools to determine whether an AI system meets its design requirements and is sufficient for its intended use. \\u201cZero drafts\\u201d are preliminary, stakeholder-
driven drafts of standards that are as thorough as possible and will be submitted into the private sector-led standardization process.\\n...\\n- The AI Evaluation and Measurement Methods Task Group
will identify and prioritize gaps, barriers and open questions across the field of AI evaluation science based on input from a range of organization types, sectors and stakeholder roles.\\n...\\n- The

NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/nist-joins-national-genesis-mission-accelerate-ai-innovation\\n\\n# NIST Joins National Genesis Mission to Accelerate AI Innovation\\n\\nAugust
4, 2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nCredit: amgun/Shutterstock\\n\\nGAITHERSBURG, Md. \\u2014 The U.S. Department of Commerce\\u2019s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the U.S.
Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science have signed a memorandum of under\", \"highlights\": [\"NIST Joins National Genesis Mission to Accelerate AI Innovation |
NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/nist-joins-national-genesis-mission-accelerate-ai-innovation\\n\\n# NIST Joins National Genesis Mission to Accelerate AI Innovation\\n\\nAugust
4, 2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nCredit: amgun/Shutterstock\\n\\nGAITHERSBURG, Md. \\u2014 The U.S. Department of Commerce\\u2019s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the U.S.
Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science have signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a collaboration to use AI-accelerated innovation to address national science and technology
challenges established by the Genesis Mission. The Genesis Mission is a whole-of-government initiative, led by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, that aims to double the
productivity and impact of American science and engineering within a decade by unlocking AI-enabled scientific discovery and innovation. This MOU formalizes NIST\\u2019s commitment to that
goal.\\n\\nNIST and DOE have deep expertise and a shared interest in applying AI innovation to address critical national challenges and opportunities. The MOU will enable the two agencies to
coordinate their efforts and leverage their complementary resources within the context of the Genesis Mission in areas including biotechnology, quantum science, and materials design and
discovery.\\n\\n\\u201cOur contribution to the Genesis Mission exemplifies NIST\\u2019s ongoing commitment to advancing U.S. leadership in critical technologies that are vital to America\\u2019s
economic and national security,\\u201d said Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director Arvind Raman. \\u201cNIST is using innovative public-private partnerships to
apply advanced AI to manufacturing and cybersecurity challenges, with initiatives aimed at rapidly delivering high-impact solutions that can be readily transitioned to the private
sector.\\u201d\\n\\nNIST will execute two of its efforts in support of the Genesis Mission through its Centers for AI in Manufacturing and Critical Infrastructure, a public-private partnership with
the nonprofit MITRE Corporation that aims to advance the delivery of AI-based technology solutions to U.S. industry. These efforts will target the Genesis Mission\\u2019s national science and
technology challenges. Additional areas of collaboration are also being discussed.\\n\\nFirst, NIST\\u2019s AI Economic Security Center for U.S. Manufacturing Productivity aims to accelerate
development and adoption of AI-driven autonomous agents for increased U.S. manufacturing productivity. It uses advanced, AI-based \\u201chuman in the loop\\u201d robotics and autonomous systems to
produce cost-competitive, high-value, customizable American products. This center has launched a project that will focus on producing drones for civilian and military applications, with the goal of
using AI to scale up production capabilities tenfold in two years. This initiative aligns with the Genesis Mission challenge \\u201cReenvisioning Advanced Manufacturing and Industrial
Productivity.\\u201d\\n\\nSecond, NIST\\u2019s AI Economic Security Center to Secure U.S. Critical Infrastructure from Cyberthreats will accelerate development and adoption of AI-based agents for
ultra-high-speed cyberthreat detection and remediation. This initiative focuses on protecting and securing critical infrastructure including power grids, telecommunications networks, water treatment
facilities, financial platforms and healthcare systems. This initiative aligns with several of the Genesis Mission challenges aimed at protecting the nation from emerging threats.\\n\\nBoth
initiatives are designed as two-year sprints that aim to rapidly produce high-impact results for commercial and industrial deployment while also yielding generalizable strategies that can be
replicated across other manufacturing and cybersecurity domains.\\n\\nReleased August 4, 2026, Updated August 5, 2026\\n\\nWas this page helpful?\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-04T00:00:00.000\",
\"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"'Spooky' Particles Transit DC Suburbs, a Step Toward ...\", \"url\": \"https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/spooky-particles-transit-dc-suburbs-step-toward-
quantum-network\", \"snippet\": \"\\u2018Spooky\\u2019 Particles Transit DC Suburbs, a Step Toward a Quantum Network | NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/spooky-particles-transit-
dc-suburbs-step-toward-quantum-network\\n\\n# \\u2018Spooky\\u2019 Particles Transit DC Suburbs, a Step Toward a Quantum Network\\n\\nAugust 5, 2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\n- Quantum networks could
supercharge scientific research, quantum computing and secure communications, but scientists must first find ways to protect fragile \\u201centangled\\u201d quantum states of photons \\u2014 particles
of\", \"highlights\": [\"\\u2018Spooky\\u2019 Particles Transit DC Suburbs, a Step Toward a Quantum Network | NIST\\n...\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08/spooky-particles-transit-dc-
suburbs-step-toward-quantum-network\\n...\\n# \\u2018Spooky\\u2019 Particles Transit DC Suburbs, a Step Toward a Quantum Network\\n...\\nAugust 5, 2026\\n...\\n- Quantum networks could supercharge
scientific research, quantum computing and secure communications, but scientists must first find ways to protect fragile \\u201centangled\\u201d quantum states of photons \\u2014 particles of light
\\u2014 as they zip through optical fibers.\\n- NIST researchers and their collaborators sent entangled photons through 62 kilometers (about 38.5 miles) of commercial fiber from the agency\\u2019s
Gaithersburg campus to the University of Maryland in College Park.\\n- The achievement shows that fragile quantum entanglement can survive even in tough, real-world conditions.\\n...\\nIn early 2025,
special signals wended their way through a fiber-optic highway strung above the streets and sidewalks of the Maryland suburbs. The arrival of those signals at their destination marks a significant
step toward a long-held dream of building a \\u201cquantum network.\\u201d Researchers believe that this emerging technology could someday link quantum devices in ways that supercharge scientific
research, enable ultrasecure communications and boost the power of future quantum computers.\\n...\\nNational Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) researchers and collaborators reported this
advance in the Journal of Optical Communications and Networking.\\n...\\nresearchers used a commercial\\n...\\nOne photon from each pair was directed to an analyzer in the NIST lab, which measured the
photon\\u2019s polarization. The other traveled through 62 kilometers (about 38.5 miles) of fiber to a second lab at the University of Maryland in College Park.\\n...\\nThe researchers knew that if
they didn\\u2019t protect the flying photons\\u2019 quantum states, the fiber would twist and distort them, ruining the entanglement. So the scientists deployed a pair of devices to stabilize the
photons\\u2019 polarizations in real time. These devices, developed by Qunnect, sent beams of \\u201creference\\u201d light through the fiber and, at the other end, measured how their polarization
states had been transformed. The exact inverse of these transformations were then applied to the experimental photons, keeping them entangled.\\n...\\nThe scientists managed to transmit 1,500
entangled photons per second, a respectable rate though one that would need to improve for quantum networks to become practical. Over a 24-hour period, the researchers were able to distribute
entangled photons 92.8% of the time, needing only 7.2% of the time for correcting polarizations. A statistical test confirmed that the photons detected at each end of the fiber had indeed remained
entangled.\\n...\\n\\u201cI would call this a stress test of quantum networking systems,\\u201d says Yicheng Shi, a physicist at NIST and the study\\u2019s lead author. \\u201cWe put this to an
extreme test in an environment that\\u2019s really noisy. Amazingly, it turned out it still worked. It\\u2019s a demonstration that quantum networking protocols can work in real-world
environments.\\u201d\\n...\\nPaper: Yicheng Shi, Jing Su, Anouar Rahmouni, Pranish Shrestha, Mheni Merzouki, Gabriel Bello Portmann, Anne Lazenby, Mael Flament, Mehdi Namazi, Abdella Battou, Oliver
Slattery and Thomas Gerrits. Entanglement Distribution Over a Polarization-Stabilized Aerial Fiber. Journal of Optical Communications and Networking. Published online July 15, 2026. DOI:
10.1364/JOCN.592521\\n...\\nReleased August 5, 2026, Updated August 6, 2026\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-05T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Back to Basics: Foundational

also largely under-resourced when it comes to building strong cyber defenses. The efficient use, or prioritization, of limited res\", \"highlights\": [\"Back to Basics: Foundational Cybersecurity
Practices for Small Businesses | NIST\\n...\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/events/2026/08/back-basics-foundational-cybersecurity-practices-small-businesses\\n...\\n# Back to Basics: Foundational
Cybersecurity Practices for Small Businesses\\n...\\nThe small business community is a large portion of the U.S. and global economy and is also largely under-resourced when it comes to building strong
cyber defenses. The efficient use, or prioritization, of limited resources is critical. Speakers from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation
(FBI), and National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) will share how to identify cybersecurity risks that small businesses commonly face and will share practical and actionable
cybersecurity safeguards that can significantly reduce cybersecurity risks and that typically do not take significant time, financial investment, or technical expertise to implement.\\n...\\n- Colleen
P. Ferranti , Assistant Section Chief, Cyber Engagement & Intelligence Section, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)\\n- Christine Serrano Glassner, Chief External Affairs Officer, Cybersecurity and
Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)\\n- Daniel Eliot, Lead for Small Business Engagement, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)\\n...\\nCreated July 14, 2026, Updated August 4,

genesis-mission-ai-partnership\", \"snippet\": \"US turns to AI agents for drone production and cyber defence | Digital Watch Observatory\\n\\n6 Aug 2026\\n\\n# US turns to AI agents for drone
production and cyber defence\\n\\nThrough the Genesis Mission AI partnership, NIST will develop autonomous agents for factories and critical-infrastructure cybersecurity.\\n\\nThe US National
Institute of Standards and Technology and Department of Energy have formed a partnership to apply AI to scientific research, manufacturing and critical infrastructure security.\\n\\nA \",
\"highlights\": [\"US turns to AI agents for drone production and cyber defence | Digital Watch Observatory\\n...\\n6 Aug 2026\\n...\\n# US turns to AI agents for drone production and cyber
defence\\n...\\nThrough the Genesis Mission AI partnership, NIST will develop autonomous agents for factories and critical-infrastructure cybersecurity.\\n...\\nThe US National Institute of Standards
and Technology and Department of Energy have formed a partnership to apply AI to scientific research, manufacturing and critical infrastructure security.\\n...\\nTwo NIST initiatives will be conducted
through AI centres operated in partnership with the nonprofit MITRE Corporation.\\n...\\nThe first will develop autonomous AI agents, human-supervised robotics and other systems intended to improve
manufacturing productivity. An initial project will examine whether AI can help increase US production capacity for civilian and military drones tenfold within two years.\\n...\\nThe second initiative
will develop AI agents capable of detecting and addressing cyber threats at extremely high speeds. Targeted infrastructure includes power grids, telecommunications networks, water treatment
facilities, financial platforms and healthcare systems.\\n...\\nNIST said public-private partnerships would help transfer resulting technologies into the US industry. Further areas of collaboration
between NIST and the Department of Energy remain under discussion.\\n...\\nThe announcement does not specify project funding, participating companies or how progress towards the drone-production
target will be measured.\\n...\\nThe partnership places autonomous AI agents at the centre of US industrial and security policy, connecting federal research with domestic manufacturing and the
protection of critical infrastructure. Its success will depend on whether ambitious targets produce independently tested and safely deployable systems rather than remaining experimental government
projects.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-06T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"2064 Calibration Method Validation | NIST\", \"url\": \"https://www.nist.gov/news-

agencies-join-genesis-mission-to-further-ai-enabled-research/\", \"snippet\": \"More Agencies Join Genesis Mission to Further AI-Enabled Research | GovCIO Media & Research\\n\\nSkip to Main
Content\\n\\n## All Topics\\n\\nAll Topics\\n\\n## Featured\\n\\n### Who\\u2019s in Charge of AI at Top Federal Agencies\\n\\n7m read\\n\\n### Implementing Agentic AI in Federal Government\\n\\n24m
watch\\n\\n### Securing Data Against Evolving Cyber Threats\\n\\n20m read\\n\\n### Topics\\n\\nTopics\\n\\nAll Topics\\n\\n### Events\\n\\nEvents\\n\\n### Videos\\n\\nVideos\\n\\n###
Podcasts\\n\\nPodcasts\\n\\n### Insights\\n\\nInsights\\n\\n# More Agencies Join Genesis Mission to Fur\", \"highlights\": [\"# More Agencies Join Genesis Mission to Further AI-Enabled
Research\\n...\\nMon, 08/10/2026\\n...\\nSeveral agencies including DOW, HHS, NIST and DHS announced their roles in advancing scientific discovery with AI through the Genesis Mission.\\n...\\nThe
Energy Department\\u2019s Genesis Mission has expanded into a governmentwide scientific research initiative, with NASA, the War Department, the Department of Health and Human Services, the National
Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Department of Homeland Security joining the AI-powered effort to accelerate discovery and unify supercomputing nationally.\\n...\\nThis brings
participation to more than 15 agencies, representing roughly $5 billion in research investments from the White House while increasing the number of National Science and Technology Challenges supported
through Genesis from 26 to 33. The new challenges include AI for biomedical research, national security, space exploration and more in line with the Office of Science and Technology Policy\\u2019s R&D
priorities for fiscal year 2028.\\n...\\n## Agencies Expand AI Research Through\\n...\\nOne of the newest agencies to join is the Department of Homeland Security\\u2019s Science and Technology
Directorate, which joined the initiative in July. Its goal is to strengthen software assurance and critical infrastructure resilience using shared AI capabilities developed through
Genesis.\\n...\\nThe National Institute of Standards and Technology is the latest agency to join the initiative. Its goal is to develop AI agents for cyberthreat detection and response. Through the
Centers for AI in Manufacturing and Critical Infrastructure, a partnership between NIST and MITRE, researchers will evaluate AI agents to help secure electric grids, telecommunications networks, water
systems and healthcare infrastructure.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-10T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"NIST National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled
for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026\", \"url\": \"https://www.einpresswire.com/article/934018342/nist-national-construction-safety-team-advisory-committee-meeting-scheduled-for-sept-23-and-24-2026\",
\"snippet\": \"NIST National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026 \\n\\n# NIST National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled
for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026\\n\\n National Institute of Standards and Technology \\n\\n August 13, 2026, 22:02 GMT \\n\\nNCST investigators monitor the progress of a structural engineering test in June
2025 as part of the Champlain Towers South investigation. Credit: NIST \\n\\nThe National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)\", \"highlights\": [\"NIST National Construction Safety Team
Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026 \\n\\n# NIST National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026\\n\\n National Institute of
Standards and Technology \\n\\n August 13, 2026, 22:02 GMT \\n\\nNCST investigators monitor the progress of a structural engineering test in June 2025 as part of the Champlain Towers South
investigation. Credit: NIST \\n\\nThe National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) will provide updates on its building failure investigations and related activities during a virtual meeting
of the National Construction Safety Team (NCST) Advisory Committee on Sept. 23 and 24, 2026. During this public meeting, NIST team members will highlight progress on their investigations into the
impacts of Hurricane Maria on Puerto Rico and the partial collapse of the Champlain Towers South building in Surfside, Florida. They will also provide an update on NIST\\u2019s Disaster and Failure
Studies Program and detail their responses to the advisory committee\\u2019s 2025 recommendations.\\n...\\nAnyone wishing to attend the virtual meeting must register by 5 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, Sept.
16, 2026. Registered attendees who wish to speak during the public comment period may sign up to do so by selecting \\u201cyes\\u201d to the public comment question on the registration form.
Additional details are available in the Federal Register notice. The full meeting agenda is available on the NIST website. \\n\\nIn June 2026, NIST released a video detailing its technical findings on
the cause of the Champlain Towers South collapse. \\n\\nAll other previously released materials relating to these investigations are available on the Hurricane Maria and Champlain Towers South
websites.\\n...\\n# NIST National Construction Safety Team Advisory Committee Meeting Scheduled for Sept. 23 and 24, 2026\\n\\n August 13, 2026, 22:02 GMT \\n\\n EIN Presswire's priority is author

(CAISI) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the General Services Administration (GSA) to support the AI\", \"highlights\": [\"CAISI signs MOU with GSA to boost AI evaluation science in
federal procurement through USAi | NIST\\n...\\n# CAISI signs MOU with GSA to boost AI evaluation science in federal procurement through USAi\\n...\\nThe Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)
has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the General Services Administration (GSA) to support the AI evaluation needs of USAi, a secure generative AI platform and centralized procurement toolbox
that enables federal agencies to confidently adopt AI at scale.\\n...\\nGSA provides centralized procurement and shared services for the federal government. Through USAi, GSA expands the federal
government\\u2019s AI infrastructure via shared services for agencies to experiment with and adopt AI systems.\\n...\\nCAISI supports AI stakeholders by developing methods to measure the capabilities
and security of leading AI models with gold-standard measurement science. CAISI will leverage its measurement expertise to help GSA and its partner agencies develop robust methodologies to evaluate
performance, security, and functionality within real-world user workflows in the USAi platform.\\n...\\n\\\"We're at a pivotal time in the AI revolution and this partnership between CAISI and GSA will
enable federal agencies to adopt AI in ways that help the American people,\\u201d said Deputy Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and Acting NIST Director Craig Burkhardt.
\\u201cWe are excited to help advance AI in support of the Trump Administration\\u2019s vision for innovation.\\u201d\\n...\\nThis partnership will further GSA and CAISI\\u2019s work to create
resources that support federal agencies\\u2019 procurement and adoption of AI systems\\u2014including methodological guidelines for pre-deployment assessments and tools enabling agencies to measure
post-deployment performance in line with their distinct missions and operations.\\n...\\nBuilding on CAISI\\u2019s ongoing work with leading AI companies and with other government partners, this
collaboration advances America\\u2019s AI Action Plan, which charges CAISI with supporting \\u201cthe development of the science of measuring and evaluating AI models\\u201d and publishing guidelines

\"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities | NIST\", \"url\": \"https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/07/uk-aisi-caisi-preliminary-
assessment-kimi-k3s-cyber-capabilities\", \"snippet\": \"UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities | NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/07/uk-aisi-caisi-
preliminary-assessment-kimi-k3s-cyber-capabilities\\n\\n# UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities\\n\\nJuly 23, 2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nThe UK Artificial Intelligence
Security Institute (UK AISI) and the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) (UK AISI / CAISI) conducted a joint evaluation of Moonshot AI\\u2019s latest model, Kimi K3 (rel\",
\"highlights\": [\"UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities | NIST\\n...\\n# UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities\\n...\\nThe UK
Artificial Intelligence Security Institute (UK AISI) and the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) (UK AISI / CAISI) conducted a joint evaluation of Moonshot AI\\u2019s latest model,
Kimi K3 (released on July 16, 2026 and slated for open-weight release by July 27, 2026). This evaluation focused on Kimi K3's cyber capabilities and found that:\\n...\\n- Kimi K3 performs
significantly below the most recent frontier cyber-capable models on preliminary cyber evaluations run by UK AISI / CAISI. Specifically:\\n...\\n- When tasked to attack a simulated corporate network
(\\u201cThe Last Ones\\u201d), Kimi K3 performs significantly below\\n...\\nmost recent frontier cyber-capable models. Specifically, on average, Kimi K3 reached step 17 of this 32-step attack path,
while the most cyber-capable U.S. models reached 28.5 steps on average.\\n...\\n- Kimi K3 performs above GLM-5.2 on the same preliminary cyber evaluations run by UK AISI / CAISI (Figure 2).\\n...\\n-
Kimi K3\\u2019s safeguards allow assistance with agentic cyber exploit development. Kimi K3's safeguards did not prevent it from attempting cyber exploit development or offensive cyber operations
during UK AISI / CAISI's evaluations.\\n...\\nThese results represent preliminary evaluations on a small set of public and private benchmarks. U.S. closed-weight models were evaluated with system-
level safeguards disabled to reduce refusals and enable measurement of maximal capabilities. Publicly available versions of these models have these safeguards enabled. Due to the specifics of Kimi
K3\\u2019s hosting setup, UK AISI / CAISI ran a selective set of cyber evaluations. Detailed methodologies are provided in individual sections.\\n...\\nThe cyber capability of models is aggregated
across multiple tasks from multiple benchmarks using an approach inspired by Item Response Theory (IRT). For details of the methodology please see prior published reports. Kimi K3\\u2019s overall
cyber capability has a larger confidence interval than other models because it was estimated from a single benchmark (ExploitBench, which has 41 tasks focused on exploit development). ExploitBench is
a leading benchmark to measure a model\\u2019s ability to progress along the software exploitation ladder. All other models\\u2019 overall cyber capability scores were derived from a larger number of
tasks that covered additional domains of cyber capability.\\n...\\nExploitBench is a public benchmark, developed by Carnegie Mellon University, that measures a model\\u2019s ability to progress along
the software exploitation ladder, including coverage and crash reproduction, arbitrary read/write, control flow hijack, and arbitrary code execution. The benchmark tests models on 41 recent
(post-2023) vulnerabilities in the V8 engine (the JavaScript and WebAssembly software that powers Chrome).\\n...\\nKimi K3 outperforms GLM-5.2, the most cyber-capable open-weight model as of June
2026. Kimi K3 achieves a score of 32%, whereas GLM-5.2 achieves a score of 24% (Figure 1).\\n...\\nUnlike the most cyber-capable models, Kimi K3 failed to develop exploits that achieved arbitrary code
execution (ACE) for ExploitBench tasks. ACE is the highest-severity outcome in exploit development, granting attackers the ability to hijack a target. Kimi K3 achieved ACE on 0/41 samples, whereas the
most cyber-capable models achieved ACE on 20/41 samples on average (Figure 3).\\n...\\n\\u201cThe Last Ones\\u201d (TLO) cyber range is a 32-step simulated corporate network attack spanning 4 subnets
and approximately 20 hosts, which would take a human expert roughly 20 hours to complete. Cyber ranges are expert-built, simulated networks of hosts, services, and vulnerabilities arranged into
sequential attack chains that begin at the point of initial network access, and can be used to measure a model's ability to conduct end-to-end cyberattacks autonomously.\\n...\\nOn this evaluation,
Kimi K3 performs significantly below the leading U.S. cyber capable models. Specifically, Kimi K3 reached step 17 of this 32-step attack path on average, while the most cyber-capable U.S. models
reached 28.5 steps on average.\\n...\\nKimi K3 outperforms GLM-5.2, the most cyber-capable open-weight model as of June 2026. Within the 100M-token limit, Kimi K3 reaches step 17 on average, compared
with step 11 for GLM-5.2.\\n...\\nIn one of the 10 attempts, Kimi K3 successfully completes \\u201cThe Last Ones\\u201d cyber range within the 100M token limit. This indicates that Kimi K3 is capable
of autonomously attacking small, weakly defended and vulnerable enterprise systems, when directed to do so and given initial network access. However, TLO differs from real-world environments in
several ways. It lacks active defenders and defensive tooling, imposes no penalty for actions that would trigger security alerts, and contains an intentional attack path.\\n...\\nSolves of TLO are no
longer exclusive to a small set of models. In prior testing, four publicly released closed-weight models have solved TLO, with the most capable models solving it more reliably at 6/10 and 7/10
attempts. Kimi K3 solved it in 1/10 attempts within the standard 100M token limit.\\n...\\nReleased July 23, 2026, Updated August 12, 2026\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-07-23T00:00:00.000\",
\"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Announcement: CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined to Enable Secure AI Evaluations | NIST\", \"url\": \"https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/03/announcement-caisi-
signs-crada-openmined-enable-secure-ai-evaluations\", \"snippet\": \"Announcement: CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined to Enable Secure AI Evaluations | NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/news-
events/news/2026/03/announcement-caisi-signs-crada-openmined-enable-secure-ai-evaluations\\n\\n# Announcement: CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined to Enable Secure AI Evaluations\\n\\nMarch 27,
2026\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nThe Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) has signed a collaborative research and development agreement (CRADA) with OpenMined, a 501(c)(3) non-profit that develops
open-source so\", \"highlights\": [\"Announcement: CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined to Enable Secure AI Evaluations | NIST\\n...\\n# Announcement: CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined to Enable Secure AI
Evaluations\\n...\\nThe Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) has signed a collaborative research and development agreement (CRADA) with OpenMined, a 501(c)(3) non-profit that develops open-
source software infrastructure for secure computation across organizational boundaries. Under this agreement, CAISI and OpenMined will collaborate on research into privacy-preserving methods for
conducting AI evaluations, enabling rigorous measurement of AI systems even when the underlying data, models, or benchmarks must remain confidential due to, for example, intellectual property
concerns, data protection requirements, or national security considerations.\\n...\\nAccess to real-world or sensitive data presents a challenge for researchers as AI evaluations are increasingly
intended to reflect or predict real-world deployments. It is simultaneously crucial that data is shared in a secure and decentralized manner, in order to safeguard intellectual property, encourage
innovation, and maintain privacy.\\n...\\nThis collaboration will leverage OpenMined\\u2019s software infrastructure, including PySyft and subsequent advances, to conduct evaluations that address both
the security requirements of AI developers and data owners, as well as the scientific rigor demanded by researchers and evaluators.\\n...\\nThe insights generated from this collaboration will support
NIST's efforts in AI security and applied AI evaluation. This research will inform the development of voluntary standards, best practices, and future recommendations for AI practitioners and adopters
on how to effectively measure AI systems, e.g., for workforce or productivity uplift and other impacts.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-03-27T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"NIST
