security/\", \"snippet\": \"NIST agentic AI initiative looks to get handle on security | Federal News Network\\n\\n# NIST agentic AI initiative looks to get handle on security\\n\\nBefore AI agents
run amok, a new NIST project is seeking feedback on the secure use of the fast evolving technology.\\n\\nFebruary 20, 2026 6:44 pm\\n\\n3 min read\\n\\nThe National Institutes of Standards and
Technology is launching a new project around standards for artificial intelligence agents, with NIST positioning the project as key to advancing agentic AI i\", \"highlights\": [\"The National
Institutes of Standards and Technology is launching a new project around standards for artificial intelligence agents, with NIST positioning the project as key to advancing agentic AI
innovation.\\n...\\nNIST\\u2019s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) announced the \\u201cAI Agent Standards Initiative\\u201d this week. The project aims to foster \\u201cindustry-led
technical standards and protocols that build public trust in AI agents, catalyze an interoperable agent ecosystem, and diffuse their benefits to all Americans and across the world,\\u201d NIST said in
a release this week.\\n...\\n\\u201cAI agents can now work autonomously for hours, write and debug code, manage emails and calendars, and shop for goods, among other emerging use cases,\\u201d NIST
added. \\u201cWhile the productivity promise is enticing, the real-world utility of\\n...\\nis constrained by their ability to interact with external systems and internal data. Absent\\n...\\nof AI
agents and interoperability among agents and digital resources, innovators may face a fragmented ecosystem and stunted adoption.\\u201d\\n...\\nWhile NIST\\u2019s press release positioned the project
around innovation, the initiative\\u2019s opening products are centered on security. Since AI agents can take actions autonomously, tech experts say they present significant safety and security
concerns.\\n...\\nThe initiative\\u2019s initial outputs includes a request for information on \\u201cAI agent security.\\u201d The deadline for responses to the RFI is March 9.\\n...\\n\\u201cCAISI
effort to understand ecosystem perspectives on current threats, mitigations, measures, and other considerations related to agent security,\\u201d NIST wrote on its website.\\n...\\nNIST\\u2019s
National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence also released a draft concept paper on \\u201cSoftware and AI Agent Identity and Authorization.\\u201d Feedback on the paper is due April 2.\\n...\\nThe
goal of the project is to explore how standards can \\u201cidentify, manage, and authorize access and actions taken by software agents, including AI agents, and provide practical guidelines for
organizations to securely implement AI agents and benefit from their improved productivity, efficiency, and decision-making,\\u201d the NCCoE wrote.\\n...\\nThe work at CAISI on agentic AI standards
is expected to be critical as the Trump administration and Congress weigh a broader approach to AI regulations.\\n...\\nMichael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and
Technology Policy has said previously that CAISI is a \\u201cvery important part of the larger AI agenda.\\u201d A top House lawmaker is developing legislation to codify the center into
law.\\n...\\n\\u201cIt\\u2019s absolutely important that the legacy work around standards relating to AI are undertaken by CAISI, and that\\u2019s what they\\u2019re challenged to do,\\u201d Kratsios
said in a January House hearing. \\u201cAnd that\\u2019s the focus that they should have, because the great standards that are put out by CAISI and by NIST are the ones that, ultimately, will empower
the proliferation of this technology across many industries.\\u201d\\n...\\nThe NIST center is expected to play a key role in setting standards for \\u201cadvanced metrology of model
evaluation,\\u201d Kratsios said.\\n...\\n\\u201cThat is something that can be used across all industries when they want to deploy these models,\\u201d he said. \\u201cYou want to have trust in them
so that when everyday Americans are using, whether it be medical models or anything else, they are comfortable with the fact that it has been tested and evaluated.\\u201d\\n...\\nThe Biden
administration initially established CAISI as the \\u201cAI Safety Institute.\\u201d The Trump administration rebranded the center, arguing it should focus on standards and innovation.\"],

NIST\\u2019s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and Info\", \"highlights\": [\"New Report: Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models | NIST\\n...\\nImproving the validity
and robustness of AI system evaluations is an ongoing goal of NIST AI measurement science efforts. A new publication from NIST\\u2019s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and Information
Technology Laboratory (ITL) aims to help advance the statistical validity of AI benchmark evaluations: NIST AI 800-3 Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models.\\n...\\nIn NIST AI
800-3, we develop a statistical model for AI evaluations which formalizes evaluation assumptions and measurement targets. Contributions include the following:\\n...\\ndistinguish two measures of
performance \\u2014 benchmark accuracy (performance on the set\\n...\\nquestions included in\\n...\\ngeneralized accuracy (performance across the broader universe\\n...\\nsimilar to those\\n...\\n).
Benchmark and generalized accuracy may meaningfully\\n...\\ndifferent ways, as depicted in the figure\\n...\\n- In addition to reviewing and expanding existing methods to estimate these accuracy
metrics, we demonstrate an approach based on generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). GLMMs are an established technique in other fields yet not commonly employed among AI evaluators.\\n...\\n- GLMMs
enable evaluators to estimate latent AI system capabilities and gain useful insights into benchmark composition and LLM performance. In many cases, GLMMs more precisely quantify the uncertainty of LLM
performance measurements compared to current techniques. We illustrate the advantages of the GLMM approach using data from the evaluation of 22 frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) on three common
LLM benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond, BIG-Bench Hard, and Global-MMLU Lite.\\n...\\nThese results are relevant to evaluators, practitioners, procurers, and developers of AI systems who are looking to better
understand and communicate AI performance from a rigorous and principled statistical perspective. Our statistical framework and techniques demonstrate an expansion of the current toolbox of evaluation
practices, providing a pathway towards increased robustness in AI measurement and deeper understanding of widely-relied-upon benchmarks.\\n...\\nsingle metric can\\n...\\nFirst, how
well\\n...\\nsimilar to those\\n...\\ncorresponding to each\\n...\\n: benchmark accuracy and generalized\\n...\\nWe show that these accuracy estimands require different estimation methods in order to
properly quantify uncertainty. Evaluators often estimate accuracy via \\u201cregression-free\\u201d methods \\u2013 in particular, computing accuracy as the grand mean of question scores \\u2013
though they may fail to clarify which notion of accuracy (generalized or benchmark) they are targeting. NIST AI 800-3 compares these regression-free approaches to an alternative using generalized
linear mixed models, akaGLMMs.\\n...\\nUsing both real and simulated benchmark data, we show that when well specified, GLMMs produce similar generalized accuracy point estimates to a regression-free
approach while more efficiently estimating uncertainty, as illustrated in the figure above. GLMMs rely on more assumptions about benchmark data than regression-free methods, but also provide some
means of checking these assumptions \\u2013 which can help surface issues with benchmark design.\\n...\\nStatistical modeling can equip evaluators with important context on evaluation results. GLMMs
produce explanatory statistics that can improve evaluators' understanding of benchmark composition and LLM performance, including estimation of latent LLM capability measures and benchmark question
difficulties. For example, question difficulty estimates (illustrated below for GPQA-Diamond) can help identify potentially problematic questions and reveal benchmark-level patterns.\\n...\\nenable
decomposition of the total variance in evaluation results into a between-question component reflecting differences in LL\\n...\\nperformance between different questions, and a within-question
component reflecting inconsistency in LLM performance on the same question. We use BIG-Bench Hard and Global-\\n...\\nMLU Lite as examples of the utility of such decomposition\\n...\\nilluminating
differences between tasks and languages. For instance, a set\\n...\\ntested LLMs scored roughly 83% on average on two BIG-Bench Hard tasks: \\u201c Penguins in a Table\\u201d, which consists of
word\\n...\\nMs to decide\\n...\\nfor each individual Table question than\\n...\\nperformance between Table\\n...\\nNIST AI 800-3 argues that the statistical validity of LLM evaluations benefits from
evaluators explicitly adopting a model for analyzing evaluation results and disclosing related assumptions. Generalized linear mixed modeling is one promising approach which could form a foundation
for more principled AI evaluation statistics. Future CAISI and NIST publications will further explore the application of statistical models to AI evaluation. We look forward to engaging with industry
and the scientific community as research on this topic continues to develop. Questions and comments can be directed to NISTAI800-3 [at] nist.gov (NISTAI800-3[at]nist[dot]gov).\\n...\\nReleased

anytime.\\n\\nInforma TechTarget |\\n\\nExplore our brands An Informa TechTarget Publication\\n\\n## People also \", \"highlights\": [\"# NIST will test three major tech firms\\u2019 frontier AI
models for cybersecurity risks\\n...\\nAfter Anthropic\\u2019s announcement of Claude Mythos, agencies across the government are racing to get ahead of new AI models\\u2019 potential
dangers.\\n...\\nThe U.S. government\\u2019s AI security center will evaluate frontier models from Google, Microsoft and xAI before their release to determine whether the models\\u2019 advanced
capabilities pose cybersecurity risks.\\n...\\nThe newly announced plan for the National Institute of Standards and Technology\\u2019s (NIST) Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) to conduct
\\u201cpre-deployment evaluations\\u201d represents the U.S. government\\u2019s most significant attempt yet to get ahead of security threats from powerful AI systems.\\n...\\n\\u201cIndependent,
rigorous measurement science is essential to understanding frontier AI and its national security implications,\\u201d CAISI Director Chris Fall said in a statement. \\u201cThese expanded industry
collaborations help us scale our work in the public interest at a critical moment.\\u201d\\n...\\nNIST said the partnerships would help the agency and the tech companies exchange information, spur
\\u201cvoluntary product improvements\\u201d and ensure the government had a \\u201cclear understanding\\u201d of what AI models were capable of doing. An interagency task force at CAISI will allow
officials from across the government to test the models, including in classified settings.\\n...\\npost that tech companies couldn\\u2019t conduct \\u201cevaluations tied to national security

focus for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), as part of our mission to measure and improve the security of AI systems. A year ago, we released a blog post detailing our efforts to
improve agent hijacking evaluations. And more recently, our evaluation of DeepSeek models showed that these models remain more vulnerable than leading U.S. models to hijacking attacks, uncovering
cases where DeepSeek models were more easily tricked into sending phishing emails, running malware, and exfiltrating user login credentials.\\n...\\nRed-teaming competitions provide a key method to
bridge this gap. In these competitions, human red-teamers are brought together to try to attack real models and defenses, providing a better opportunity to measure how these defenses will hold up
against real-world adversaries.\\n...\\nThe results of these competitions provide valuable information about the robustness of current models, as well as data and insights that can be used to improve
future security evaluations. That\\u2019s why CAISI partnered with Gray Swan, the UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI), and several frontier AI labs to analyze the data from a recent large-scale public
red-teaming competition.\\n...\\nThe paper draws upon data from a public red-teaming competition hosted by Gray Swan, which challenged participants to develop hijacking attacks against 13 different
frontier models in a variety of different agentic scenarios, including tool use agents, coding agents, and computer use agents.\\n...\\nAcross more than 250,000 attack attempts from over 400
participants, at least one successful attack was found against all of the target frontier models, highlighting the ongoing challenge that hijacking attacks pose for secure agent use.\\n...\\nHowever,
the data also showed that frontier models differed sharply in how many successful attacks were found \\u2013 and also found that this did not correlate uniformly with model capability \\u2013
emphasizing how red-teaming competitions and comparative security benchmarking can help inform users of the risk profiles of different models they might adopt for agentic applications.\\n...\\nThe
paper also investigates how attacks developed against one model during the competition transferred to other models and scenarios in post-competition testing. It found certain families of
\\u201cuniversal\\u201d attacks that were often able to transfer across scenarios and models, potentially by exploiting shared underlying weaknesses in instruction-following behavior between models.
This analysis also revealed that successful attacks developed against more robust models (those with lower rates of attack success during the competition) were particularly likely to transfer to
models that were less robust, but not the other way around.\\n...\\nRed-teaming competitions are a valuable tool for improving and assessing the security of frontier models. They provide opportunities
for evaluators to better understand and analyze the kinds of attacks that dedicated adversaries can find, particularly against models that are increasingly robust to known static attacks (a key
challenge when it comes to benchmarking).\\n...\\nAs part of the research collaboration with Gray Swan, CAISI contributed to the analysis methodology for this work, and will also receive data from the

creates exposure to indirect prompt injection atta\", \"highlights\": [\"LLM based agents are increasingly deployed in high stakes settings where they process external data sources such as emails,
documents, and code repositories. This creates exposure to indirect prompt injection attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in external content manipulate agent behavior without user
awareness. A critical but underexplored dimension of this threat is concealment: since users tend to observe only an agent\\u2019s final response, an attack can conceal its existence by presenting no
clue of compromise in the final user facing response while successfully executing harmful actions. This leaves users unaware of the manipulation and likely to accept harmful outcomes as legitimate. We
present findings from a large scale public red teaming competition evaluating this dual objective across three agent settings: tool calling, coding, and computer use. The competition attracted 464
participants who submitted 272,000 attack attempts against 13 frontier models, yielding 8,648 successful attacks across 41 scenarios. All models proved vulnerable, with attack success rates ranging
from 0.5% (Claude Opus 4.5) to 8.5% (Gemini 2.5 Pro). We identify universal attack strategies that transfer across 21 of 41 behaviors and multiple model families, suggesting fundamental weaknesses in
instruction following architectures. Capability and robustness showed weak correlation, with Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibiting both high capability and high vulnerability. To address benchmark saturation and
obsoleteness, we will endeavor to deliver quarterly updates through continued red teaming competitions. We open source the competition environment for use in evaluations, along with 95 successful
attacks against Qwen that did not transfer to any closed source model. We share model-specific attack data with respective frontier labs, and the full dataset with the UK AISI and US CAISI to support
robustness research.\\n...\\nTo collect the most up to date and highest quality attacks, we hosted a large scale competition named Indirect Prompt Injection Arena collaborating with frontier labs and
government AI institutes including the UK AISI11 1 https://www.aisi.gov.uk and US CAISI22 2 https://www.nist.gov/caisi. This three-week competition had a $40k total prize pool and attracted 464 total
unique participants, who contributed 240K+ total attack attempts, 8K+ of which were successful. We observe an overall ASR ranging 0.5% to 8.5% across 13 participating models spanning major proprietary
and open-weight ones (see Figure 1).\\n...\\nOpen science effort. We open source the full evaluation kit33 3 https://github.com/grayswansecurity/ipi_arena_os along with 95 successful attacks against

with the respective frontier labs, and the full dataset with government AI institutes including the UK AISI and US CAISI to support robustness research.\\n...\\ncausing agents to execute
harmful\\n...\\noversight to observable outputs\\n...\\nIn this competition\\n...\\nwe designed 41\\n...\\nin collaboration with the UK AI Security Institute and frontier labs including OpenAI,

frontier labs. The competition ran in three waves: an initial wave 0 with 4 behaviors, followed by two main waves across a two-week period with a total of 37 behaviors. We excluded results from wave 0

\", \"highlights\": [\"Cheating On AI Agent Evaluations | NIST\\n\\nhttps://www.nist.gov/blogs/caisi-research-blog/cheating-ai-agent-evaluations\\n\\n## CAISI Research Blog\\n\\nA NIST blog from the
Center for AI Standards and Innovation\\n\\n# Cheating On AI Agent Evaluations\\n\\nDecember 2, 2025\\n\\n## Share\\n\\nBy Maia Hamin and Benjamin Edelman\\n\\nAI evaluations are designed to assess
and compare how AI models perform on different tasks. Developers, users, and independent evaluators \\u2014 like the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) \\u2014 can use evaluations to track
trends in model capabilities and inform decisions about real-world use.\\n\\nAgent evaluations test whether models can use tools in a multi-turn feedback loop to solve complex problems like debugging
software or uncovering cybersecurity vulnerabilities. They allow evaluators to measure new and increasingly economically valuable capabilities, but also bring new methodological challenges \\u2014
including, as CAISI and other evaluators have found, the risk that AI agents can use their tools to cheat.\\n\\nAs part of our mission, CAISI both directly evaluates AI models and seeks to advance
best practices for AI measurement science. To improve our evaluations, we built an AI transcript analysis tool to search through our historical evaluation transcripts for cheating. To support the
development of stronger ecosystem practices, the following pages share examples that we uncovered and suggests takeaways that may help other evaluators reduce the incidence and impact of evaluation
cheating.\\n\\nUsing our transcript analysis tool, we found several examples of how models were able to successfully cheat on agentic coding and cyber benchmarks, including:\\n\\n- Models using the
internet to find walkthroughs and answers for cyber capture-the-flag challenges\\n- Models using generic denial-of-service attacks to crash servers on cyber tasks instead of exploiting intended
vulnerabilities\\n- Models cheating on coding benchmarks by looking up more recent code versions, disabling assertions, and adding test-specific logic.\\n\\nWe bucket these examples into two
categories of cheating risks: solution contamination, where a model accesses information that improperly reveals the solution to an evaluation task; and grader gaming, where a model exploits a gap or
misspecification in an evaluation\\u2019s automated scoring system to craft a solution that scores highly without fulfilling the \\u201cspirit\\u201d of the intended task.\\n\\nExamples of evaluation
cheating from CAISI\\u2019s evaluation logs\\n\\n| CAISI Benchmark | Cheating Examples from Evaluation Logs | Cheating Type | % Logs with Successful Solution Due to Cheating (Lower Bound) |\\n| --- |
--- | --- | --- |\\n| Cybench | Using coding tools to search the internet for challenge flags and walkthroughs | Solution contamination | 0.3% |\\n| SWE-bench Verified | Reviewing more recent code
versions on GitHub Installing more recent code versions using package managers | Solution contamination | 0.1% |\\n| | Commenting out assertion checks to pass unit tests | Grader gaming | 0.2% |\\n|
CVE-Bench (Internal) | Using denial-of-service attacks to crash the target server instead of exploiting the CVE | Grader gaming | 4.80% |\\n\\nIn general, we define evaluation cheating as:\\n\\nwhen
an AI model exploits a gap between what an evaluation task is intended to measure and its implementation, solving the task in a way that subverts the validity of the measurement.\\n\\nThis definition
focuses on the problem that cheating creates for evaluation validity: if models can exploit implementation loopholes to score higher without actually improving at the skills an evaluation is intended
to measure, it degrades the value of that measurement for decisions about real-world adoption. As models become increasingly adept problem-solvers, they may be able to find new successful cheating
strategies, and detecting and preventing cheating may become increasingly important for the validity and comparability of evaluation results.\\n\\nBased on lessons we learned through this process, we
share some preliminary suggested practices for other evaluators and benchmark designers interested in addressing evaluation cheating, including:\\n\\n- Review evaluation transcripts for cheating,
including by leveraging AI transcript analysis tools that can help scale human review processes.\\n- Prevent cheating by closing task design loopholes and setting clear rules in task prompts in order
to make model comparisons more accurate and fair.\\n- Standardize benchmark-specific expectations about agent affordances and restrictions to help evaluators create more comparable evaluation results,
including by making it easier to catch and prevent cheating.\\n\\nView the full writeup to see examples of cheating from CAISI's agent evaluations and a discussion of practices to address evaluation
cheating.\\n\\nWas this page helpful?\"], \"published_date\": \"2025-12-02T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Assessment of Z.ai\\u2019s GLM-5.2\", \"url\":

\"## Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition\\n\\nAndy Zou 1,\\u00b6 ,\\u00a7 Maxwell Lin 1 Eliot Jones 1 Micha Nowak 1 Mateusz Dziemian 1 Nick
Winter 1 Alexander Grattan 1 Valent Nathanael 1 Ayla Croft 1 Xander Davies 2,\\u266f Jai Patel 2 Robert Kirk 2 Nate Burnikell 2 Yarin Gal 2,\\u266f Dan Hendrycks 1,\\u00a7 J. Zico Kolter 1,\\u00b6

advances have enabled LLM-powered AI agents to autonomously execute complex tasks by combining language model reasoning with tools, memory, and web access. But can these systems be trusted to follow
deployment policies in realistic environments, especially under attack? To investigate, we ran the largest public red-teaming competition to date, targeting 22 frontier AI agents across 44 realistic
deployment scenarios. Participants submitted 1.8 million prompt injection attacks, with over 60,000 successfully eliciting policy violations such as unauthorized data access, illicit financial
actions, and regulatory noncompliance. We use these results to build the Agent Red Teaming (ART) benchmark\\u2014a curated set of high-impact attacks\\u2014and evaluate it across 19 state-of-the-art
models. Nearly all agents exhibit policy violations for most behaviors within 10\\u2013100 queries, with high attack transferability across models and tasks. Importantly, we find limited correlation
between agent robustness and model size, capability, or inference-time compute, suggesting that additional defenses are needed against adversarial misuse. Our findings highlight critical and
persistent vulnerabilities in today\\u2019s AI agents. By releasing the ART benchmark and accompanying evaluation framework, we aim to support more rigorous security assessment and drive progress
toward safer agent deployment.\\n...\\nvulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where carefully crafted inputs cause agents to bypass intended constraints and exhibit dangerous behaviors [11, 19, 28,
47, 58, 62, 63]. Moreover, interactions with externally sourced data can result in indirect prompt injections, embedding hidden adversarial instructions\\u2014from web pages, PDFs, emails, or even
image pixels\\u2014unknowingly influencing the agent\\u2019s behavior [12, 62]. Despite the increasing recognition of these threats, our understanding of the full range of vulner abilities and real-
world performance limitations of LLM-based agents is still incomplete. Prior red-teaming and security evaluations have largely been limited in scope, often investigating simplistic chatbot
interactions or constrained classifier tasks under artificial or academic benchmark conditions [2, 15, 20, 26, 27, 45]. Consequently, comprehensive and realistic evaluations of agent deployments in
complex real-world environments are urgently needed. To address this, and evaluate the real-world robustness of AI agents, we ran a large-scale red-teaming competition targeting 44 realistic
deployment scenarios powered by 22 frontier LLMs with over $170,000 in prizes. Over a month, participants submitted more than 1.8 million adversarial prompts in sandboxed environments simulating
tools, memory, and policy constraints. The results revealed deep and recurring failures: agents frequently violated explicit policies, failed to resist adversarial inputs, and performed high-risk
actions across domains such as finance, healthcare, and customer support. These attacks proved highly transferable and generalizable, affecting models regardless of size, capability, or defense
strategies. Our evaluation provides the broadest and most current survey of real-world security risks affecting agent-based LLM deployments and active exploits employed against them. Building from
these extensive red-teaming results, we introduce an AI Agent Red Teaming benchmark, featuring prompt injections that achieve a 100% attack success rate against current state-of-the-art agents, making
it one of the most challenging AI agent security benchmarks. We plan to publicly release the test cases along with a private leaderboard to prevent overfitting to known attacks and active misuse.
Ultimately, we hope to improve the understanding of security vulnerabilities in agentic LLM deployments, advance automated red-teaming practices, and catalyze further research towards agentic LLM
systems that can reliably serve society by consistently and securely adhering to established deployment policies.\\n...\\n2.3 Agent Red Teaming Benchmark (ART) Using submissions from the red-teaming
challenge, we constructed the Agent Red Teaming (ART) Benchmark: a curated dataset of high-quality prompt injections spanning 44 distinct agent deployment settings, along with their corresponding
environments and working prompt injections. To ensure benchmark quality, we construct a refined subset of attacks from challenge submissions by first applying a stricter LLM-based judge for filtering
purposes. Prompt details are presented in the appendix. For each combination of behavior and model, we then sample up to 5 high-quality attacks. This process results in a final ART dataset containing
4,700 selected attacks across 44 target behaviors. We evaluate the effectiveness of these attacks on a comprehensive set of 19 frontier LLMs, encompassing all publicly available challenge models and
additional unseen models such as Gemini 2.5 Pro and o4-mini, neither of which were included in the original competition. Figure 4 shows attack success rates across the evaluated models. After
approximately 10 to 100 attack queries per behavior, most agents exhibit policy violations across nearly all tested behaviors, making ART a rigorous and challenging benchmark for evaluating agent
security. We intend to maintain ART as a private\"], \"published_date\": null, \"score\": null}]}"}]

issues/2026/05/05/advancing-ai-evaluation-with-the-center-for-ai-standards-us-and-innovation-and-the-ai-security-institute-uk/\", \"snippet\": \"Advancing AI evaluation with the Center for AI
Standards (US) and Innovation and the AI Security Institute (UK) - Microsoft On the Issues\\n\\nCenter for AI Standards and Innovation(CAISI) in the US and the AI Security Institute(AISI) in the UK to
advance the science of AI testing and evaluation, including through collaborative work to test Microsoft\\u2019s frontier models, assess safeguards, and help mitigate national security and large-scale
public safety risks. These agreements matter because ongoing,\", \"highlights\": [\"Advancing AI evaluation with the Center for AI Standards (US) and Innovation and the AI Security Institute (UK) -
Microsoft On the Issues\\n...\\nCenter for AI Standards and Innovation(CAISI) in the US and the AI Security Institute(AISI) in the UK to advance the science of AI testing and evaluation, including
through collaborative work to test Microsoft\\u2019s frontier models, assess safeguards, and help mitigate national security and large-scale public safety risks. These agreements matter because
ongoing, rigorous testing is essential to building trust and confidence in advanced AI systems. Well-constructed tests help us understand whether our systems are working as intended and delivering the
benefits they are designed to provide. Testing also helps us stay ahead of risks, such as AI-driven cyberattacks and other criminal misuses of AI systems, that can emerge once advanced AI systems are
deployed in the world.\\n...\\nWhile Microsoft regularly undertakes many types of AI testing on its own, testing for national security and large-scale public safety risks necessarily must be a
collaborative endeavor with governments. This type of testing depends on deep technical, scientific, and national security expertise that is uniquely held by institutions like CAISI in the US and AISI
in the UK and the government agencies they work with. By combining that government expertise with Microsoft\\u2019s experience building and deploying AI systems at global scale, together we are better
positioned to anticipate and manage national security and public safety risks in ways that build public trust and confidence in advanced AI systems.\\n...\\nAdvancing the science of AI evaluation
requires more than isolated research or one-off testing. It depends on sustained collaboration between industry, government, and research institutions. Through our new and expanded partnerships with
the US and UK governments\\u2014alongside national security\\u2013focused evaluations of model capabilities\\u2014Microsoft is bringing technical expertise and operational experience to strengthen AI
evaluation methods and practical testing foundations.\\n...\\n- In the US, with CAISI, Microsoft and NIST will collaborate on improving methodologies for adversarial assessments\\u2014testing AI
systems in ways that probe unexpected behaviors, misuse pathways, and failure modes, much like stress-testing whether airbags, seatbelts, and braking systems work effectively and reliably in safety-
critical driving scenarios. This work involves co-developing more systematic and reproducible approaches to evaluation, including shared frameworks, datasets, and workflows for assessing safety,
security, and robustness risks in advanced AI systems. It also builds on our AI Red Team\\u2019s novel research and tools to detect compromised models at scale.\\n...\\n- In the UK, with AISI,
Microsoft will collaborate on research related to frontier safety and security, including methods for evaluating high-risk capabilities and the effectiveness of the safeguards used to address them.
The partnership will also include societal resilience research examining how conversational AI systems interact with users in sensitive contexts.\\n...\\nThese collaborations are designed to improve
measurement science, evaluation methodologies, practical testing workflows, and real-world mitigation impact. They reflect a shared commitment to rigorous, practical approaches that can make
safeguards stronger and evaluations more reliable.\\n...\\nNo organization can address these challenges alone. Our partnerships with CAISI and AISI are a key part of a wider effort to build the
institutions, research base, and shared methodologies needed for effective AI testing. This effort also includes:\\n...\\n- Pursuing research and evaluation in collaboration with other AI institutes
globally while helping advance shared priorities and methodologies for testing through the International Network for AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science.\\n...\\n- Helping deliver industry best
practices through the Frontier Model Forum(FMF), an initiative dedicated to advancing the science and practice of frontier AI safety and security. Through the FMF, we are working with other leading AI
developers to support independent research, develop shared evaluation methodologies, and promote transparency around risk mitigation strategies.\\n...\\n- Contributing to MLCommons, a multistakeholder
non-profit that develops and operationalizes testing tools such as AILuminate, a family of safety and security benchmarks. In February, we announced efforts underway\\n...\\ninstitutions in India,
Japan, Korea, and Singapore to expand AILuminate to support multilingual, multicultural, and multimodal evaluation, helping to make sure that AI systems work well in the languages and cultural
contexts in which people around the world use them.\\n...\\nAs AI capabilities advance, so too must the rigor of the testing and safeguards that underpin them. We will apply what we learn from these
partnerships directly into how we design, test, and deploy AI systems, ensuring that progress in evaluation science translates into safer, more secure products for our customers. As these partnerships
progress, we will share what we learn and look for opportunities to apply insights and best practices to AI testing more broadly.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-05-05T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null},

\"highlights\": [\"## CAISI\\u2019s agreements with Google, Microsoft, and xAI preceded a report that the White House may be planning to create its own AI vetting system.\\n...\\nThe Center for AI

## 💬 Response

## NIST / CAISI AI Announcements, August 1–19, 2026

### Bottom line

**No new CAISI agreement announcements occurred between August 1 and August 19, 2026.** The CAISI "News and Updates" feed on nist.gov/caisi has published nothing new since **July 23, 2026**. The only August activity touching a CAISI page is a **content update (Aug 12) to the July 23 Kimi K3 report** — not a new item. NIST did publish AI-related news in August 2026, but all of it came from other NIST units (ITL, the Genesis Mission team, the NVD/cybersecurity program), not CAISI.

---

### 1. CAISI-specific items in the Aug 1–19 window

| Date | Item | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Aug 12, 2026** | "UK AISI / CAISI Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities" — page footer reads *"Released July 23, 2026, Updated August 12, 2026"* | **Update to an existing July item**, not a new announcement |
| — | No new CAISI news release, agreement, MOU, CRADA, RFI, or model evaluation published | — |

The current top of the CAISI News and Updates list, newest first, is: Kimi K3 (Jul 23) → GLM-5.2 (Jul 17) → DeepSeek V4 Pro (May) → OpenMined CRADA (Mar 27) → GSA MOU (Mar 18). The CAISI Research Blog's newest post is still **March 23, 2026** ("Insights into AI Agent Security from a Large-Scale Red-Teaming Competition").

### 2. NIST AI-related news releases and announcements, August 1–19, 2026

- **Aug 4, 2026 — "NIST Joins National Genesis Mission to Accelerate AI Innovation."** NIST and the DOE Office of Science signed an MOU to apply AI to national science and technology challenges under the White House OSTP-led Genesis Mission. Two efforts run through the NIST/MITRE Centers for AI in Manufacturing and Critical Infrastructure: an AI Economic Security Center for U.S. Manufacturing Productivity (drone production, goal of 10× capacity in two years) and an AI Economic Security Center to Secure U.S. Critical Infrastructure from Cyberthreats. Both are two-year sprints. *Released Aug 4, updated Aug 5.* Quoted: Under Secretary and NIST Director Arvind Raman. **This is the only NIST AI news release proper in the window.**
- **Aug 7, 2026 — TEVV-Athlon Framework (NIST AI 200-2 ipd).** Initial public draft of "The TEVV-Athlon Framework for Evaluating AI Systems," a four-stage method for building customized AI test/evaluation/verification/validation assessments. 60-day comment period opened Aug 7 and closes **Oct 6, 2026**. Page created Aug 4, updated Aug 14. DOI: 10.6028/NIST.AI.200-2.ipd. This is an ITL/AI Innovation Lab product, not CAISI.
- **Aug 12, 2026 — NVD modernization RFI.** Federal Register doc 2026-16371 (91 FR 52042), "Request for Information (RFI) on Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of Artificial Intelligence" (filed Aug 11, published Aug 12). Accompanied by a NIST Cybersecurity Insights blog, "Shaping the NVD for the Future," same date. Comments due **Oct 13, 2026**. NIST told Nextgov the RFI is *not* a response to the Gold Eagle Initiative or any executive order. Mentions a NIST AI tool in development called **V-etalon**.
- **Aug 14, 2026** — Both the NIST "AI Standards" page and the "NIST ITL AI Program" page carry an "Updated August 14, 2026" stamp. The ITL page states **"NIST launched the AI Technology Evaluation (AITE) in August 2026"** — though the AITE news release itself was **July 27, 2026** (updated July 28).

Non-AI NIST news in the same window, for completeness: "'Spooky' Particles Transit DC Suburbs" (Aug 5, quantum networking) and the NCST Advisory Committee meeting notice (Aug 13).

### 3. Immediately preceding CAISI items (for cadence)

| Date | Item | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Jul 23, 2026 | UK AISI / CAISI assessment of Kimi K3 cyber capabilities | Evaluation |
| Jul 17, 2026 | CAISI Assessment of Z.ai's GLM-5.2 (assessment completed Jul 8) | Evaluation |
| May 5, 2026 | **CAISI Signs Agreements re: Frontier AI National Security Testing with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, xAI** | **Agreement** |
| May 2026 | CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro (evaluated April 2026) | Evaluation |
| Mar 27, 2026 | **CAISI signs CRADA with OpenMined** | **Agreement** |
| Mar 18, 2026 | **CAISI signs MOU with GSA** (USAi platform) | **Agreement** |
| Feb 17, 2026 | AI Agent Standards Initiative launch | Initiative |
| Feb 13/19, 2026 | International Network consensus areas; NIST AI 800-3 | Publication |
| Jan 12, 2026 | RFI on securing AI agent systems | RFI |
| Sep 25, 2025 | CAISI works with OpenAI and Anthropic | Agreement/collab |
| Aug 29, 2024 | US AISI MOUs with Anthropic and OpenAI | Agreement |

**Agreement-type announcements in 2026: three (Mar 18, Mar 27, May 5). None since May 5, 2026** — a gap of roughly 3.5 months as of Aug 19.

### 4. Organizational context bearing on the Aug 10 – Sept 3 window

- **CAISI has no permanent director.** Chris Fall, appointed April 2026, resigned around **July 20, 2026**, after roughly three months. NIST Director **Arvind Raman** is serving as acting CAISI director. No permanent successor had been announced as of Aug 19, 2026. Fall's predecessor-designate Collin Burns was reportedly pushed out after four days.
- **Funding:** CAISI received **$10M in FY2026**, equal to the prior two fiscal years. Rep. Jay Obernolte's bipartisan bill (**H.R. 9363**) to codify CAISI provides **$20M/year**; Obernolte has said the real need is closer to **$100M/year**. OSTP Director Michael Kratsios told the House Science Committee (~July 22, 2026) that "CAISI can certainly benefit from more resources."
- **Program scale:** As of the May 5, 2026 announcement, CAISI had completed **more than 40 evaluations**, including of unreleased state-of-the-art models. All five major U.S. frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Microsoft, xAI) are under agreement.

### 5. Methodological caveats

NIST's news listing pages (`/news-events/news`, the CAISI tag page, `/artificial-intelligence`) are JavaScript-rendered and did not yield dated lists on direct fetch; `https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/08` returns HTTP 404 (not a valid listing URL). Findings above were assembled from the search index's cached full-page captures (which include the "Released … Updated …" footers), the CAISI tag page's reverse-chronological text extraction, the NIST GovDelivery bulletin archive, and Federal Register records. No Wayback snapshot of nist.gov/caisi or the CAISI tag page exists at or before 2026-08-19, so I could not independently confirm the list ordering against an archived capture. The absence of an August CAISI item is a negative finding supported by convergent sources rather than by a single authoritative dated index.

testing safeguard architectures.** They developed a sophisticated universal jailbreak that encoded harmful interactions in ways that evaded our standard detection methods. Rather than simply patching

enhances red-teaming effectiveness.** Our experience shows that giving government red-teamers deeper access to our systems enables more sophisticated vulnerability discovery. We provided several key

benchmarking.\\n- **Extensive documentation and internal resources.** We provided trusted government red-teamers with our safeguard architecture details, documented vulnerabilities, safeguards
reports, and granular content policy information (including specific prohibited requests and evaluation criteria). This transparency helped teams target high-value testing areas rather than searching

**The single most important structural fact for your base rate: this was not a same-day tri-party release.** The two companies published within ~55 minutes of each other on Sept 12; UK AISI followed on Sept 13; **NIST posted 13 days later, on Sept 25.** The NIST page describes the company posts in the past tense ("OpenAI and Anthropic *recently* published blog posts"), confirming it was a follow-on government note rather than a coordinated launch.

Note the OpenAI title differs from the phrasing in your question: the slug is `us-caisi-uk-aisi-ai-update`, but the actual headline is "Working with US CAISI and UK AISI to build more secure AI systems."

## 2. Content of the NIST page

Three short paragraphs, no data or figures of its own:

1. **Mandate framing.** Through America's AI Action Plan, President Trump tasked CAISI to collaborate with leading American AI developers to actively protect the private sector from AI security risks, including malicious cyber actors. CAISI "has assembled a leading group of scientists with expertise in machine learning and cybersecurity" and "has assisted American AI developers in this area for the last year."
2. **The announcement itself.** "Most recently, CAISI worked with OpenAI and Anthropic to identify security issues with their advanced AI systems and bolster measurement of AI security. OpenAI and Anthropic recently published blog posts describing concrete security improvements made as a result of CAISI's research and evaluations, which were completed in partnership with the UK AI Security Institute." It then links out to both company posts.
3. **Forward-looking.** CAISI and UK AISI continue collaborating on secure AI innovation, including developing best practices in metrology and standards for AI models and improving understanding of the most advanced model capabilities.

The substantive detail lives entirely in the company posts: Anthropic's covers CAISI/AISI red-teaming of its Constitutional Classifiers on Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 (prompt injection bypasses via false human-review annotations, a universal jailbreak that prompted an architectural restructure, cipher-based attacks, obfuscation attacks, automated attack refinement). OpenAI's covers two novel CAISI-found vulnerabilities in ChatGPT Agent chained into a ~50% success-rate exploit (fixed within one business day), plus UK AISI biosecurity red-teaming from May 2025 through the ChatGPT Agent (July) and GPT-5 (August) launches, yielding "more than a dozen" vulnerability reports.

## 3. Base rate: how often CAISI makes joint announcements with named frontier developers

I pulled NIST's complete CAISI-tagged news index (21 items, 2024-08-29 → 2026-07-23) plus the separately-distributed May 2026 release. Sorting by *type* matters here, because CAISI publishes far more often than it announces developer collaborations.

**Category A — joint announcements naming specific US frontier developers (the class your question is about): 3 events in ~24 months.**

| Date | Event | Companies |
|---|---|---|
| **2024-08-29** | US AI Safety Institute Signs Agreements Regarding AI Safety Research, Testing and Evaluation | Anthropic + OpenAI |
| **2025-09-25** | CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic to Promote Secure AI Innovation | OpenAI + Anthropic |
| **2026-05-05** | CAISI Signs Agreements Regarding Frontier AI National Security Testing | Google DeepMind + Microsoft + xAI |

Intervals: **392 days** (Aug 2024 → Sep 2025), then **222 days** (Sep 2025 → May 2026). Mean ≈ 307 days, i.e. roughly one every **8–10 months**. As of today (2026-08-19), **106 days** have elapsed since the most recent one.

Every one of the three is a *multi-company* announcement — CAISI has never published a collaboration announcement naming a single US developer in isolation. Note also that the May 2026 release describes its agreements as building on "previously announced partnerships, which have been **renegotiated**" — implying the OpenAI/Anthropic MOUs were reworked in that same wave, though neither company is named.

**Category B — CAISI model evaluations (much more frequent, ~every 6-10 weeks, and directed at PRC models rather than US partners):** DeepSeek (2025-09-30), Kimi K2 Thinking (2025-12-12), DeepSeek V4 Pro (2026-05-01), Z.ai GLM-5.2 (2026-07-17), UK AISI/CAISI joint on Kimi K3 (2026-07-23).

**Category C — institutional/standards output (roughly monthly):** TRAINS Taskforce (2024-11-20), agent hijacking blog (2025-01-17), consortium lessons (2025-08-05), agent security RFI (2026-01-12), benchmark best practices (2026-01-30), International Network consensus (2026-02-13), AI Agent Standards Initiative + listening sessions (2026-02-17), statistical models report (2026-02-19), deployed-system monitoring report (2026-03-09), GSA/USAi MOU (2026-03-18), OpenMined CRADA (2026-03-27).

**Related pre-deployment evaluation posts on individual US models** (a fourth, now-dormant pattern from the AISI era): Claude 3.5 Sonnet (2024-11-19) and OpenAI o1 (2024-12-18). No equivalents have been published since.

- The NIST page has **no Wayback Machine snapshot** at any date I queried (Sept 2025, Dec 2025, Aug 2026) — the archive returns "no archived snapshot." Date verification therefore rests on the live page's structured metadata, which is internally consistent across three independent fields (OpenGraph, JSON-LD, and the rendered `<time>` element).
- The **May 5, 2026 announcement does not appear in NIST's own CAISI news search index**, and the URL cited by ExecutiveGov (`/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-signs-agreements-regarding-frontier-ai-national-security-testing`) currently **404s**. The announcement is nonetheless confirmed by NIST's official GovDelivery bulletin (`content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USNIST/bulletins/415cadf`) and verbatim wire copy dated May 5, 2026. Treat the NIST page itself as possibly moved or withdrawn.
- The Aug 2024 AISI/Anthropic/OpenAI page carries `dateModified = 2026-05-04T15:30`, one day before the May 5 announcement — consistent with a coordinated content update accompanying the renegotiated agreements.
- One quantitative anchor from the May 2026 release: CAISI reported having completed **more than 40 evaluations** to date, "including on state-of-the-art models that remain unreleased." CAISI Director is **Chris Fall**.

## 💬 Response

Report delivered. Key findings:

**Dates (all from source HTML metadata, not search snippets):**
- **NIST/CAISI page: September 25, 2025** (08:00 EDT, modified 14:12 EDT same day)
- **Anthropic blog: September 12, 2025** (tweet at 20:26 UTC)
- **OpenAI post: September 12, 2025** (tweet at 21:21 UTC) — note its actual title is "Working with US CAISI and UK AISI to build more secure AI systems"; `us-caisi-uk-aisi-ai-update` is just the slug
- Bonus: UK AISI companion post, September 13, 2025

**The finding that matters most for your base rate:** this was *not* a coordinated same-day tri-party release. The companies went first (55 minutes apart), UK AISI followed next day, and NIST posted **13 days later**, referring to the company posts in past tense.

**Base rate:** CAISI/US AISI has made exactly **3 joint announcements naming specific US frontier developers in ~24 months** — 2024-08-29 (Anthropic + OpenAI), 2025-09-25 (OpenAI + Anthropic), 2026-05-05 (Google DeepMind + Microsoft + xAI). Intervals of 392 and 222 days, mean ~307 days. All three were multi-company; none named a single lab in isolation. 106 days have elapsed since the most recent.

Worth separating from the much higher-frequency categories: CAISI *model evaluations* (~every 6-10 weeks, all targeting PRC models — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM) and institutional/standards output (~monthly).

Two source caveats I'd flag: the NIST Sept 2025 page has **no Wayback snapshot at any date**, so dating rests on three internally consistent live metadata fields; and the May 2026 announcement **404s at its cited NIST URL and is absent from NIST's own CAISI news index** — confirmed instead via NIST's official GovDelivery bulletin and wire copy.

  "code": "\nimport numpy as np\nrng = np.random.default_rng(7)\nN = 400_000\n\n# Decomposition: P(YES) = P(some official federal announcement re: frontier-model eval agreements in Aug10-Sep3)\n#                        x P(covers BOTH OpenAI and Anthropic | announcement)\n#                        x P(qualifies as \"new or materially expanded\" per fine print | covers both)\n\n# --- Component 1: hazard of ANY qualifying-type official announcement in a 24-day window ---\n# Baseline: ~2 such public federal announcements in 24 months (Aug2024 AISI MOUs; May2026 CAISI agreements)\n# -> ~1.0/yr -> 24/365 * 1.0 ~= 6.6% baseline for \"an announcement of this genre\"\nbase_rate_per_year = rng.uniform(0.8, 2.0, N)          # uncertainty in genre frequency\nwindow = 24/365\np_any_base = 1 - np.exp(-base_rate_per_year*window)\n\n# Activity multiplier: framework just finalized Aug1-4, implementation phase -> elevated\n# BUT explicit WH policy of NON-publication + CAISI told to stop public reporting + no permanent director\nactivity_mult = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(2.2), sigma=0.45, size=N)   # elevated activity\nsecrecy_mult  = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(0.30), sigma=0.45, size=N)  # documented suppression of public output\np_any = np.clip(p_any_base*activity_mult*secrecy_mult, 0, 0.95)\n\n# --- Component 2: given an announcement, does it cover BOTH OpenAI and Anthropic? ---\n# May 5 2026 precedent: official announcement named the OTHER three (GDM/MSFT/xAI).\n# Per WH official, framework ALREADY applies to closed models of Anthropic+OpenAI;\n# stated expansion direction is toward OPEN models (Meta etc.) -> both-named is not the modal case.\np_both = rng.beta(3.5, 6.5, N)   # mean ~0.35\n\n# --- Component 3: meets \"new or materially expanded\" fine print (names previously-uncovered\n#     model family / access arrangement / testing scope / evaluation domain) ---\np_material = rng.beta(6, 4, N)   # mean ~0.60\n\np_yes = p_any * p_both * p_material\n\n# small additive allowance for lenient resolution (e.g. NIST posts a joint OpenAI+Anthropic\n# collaboration page like the Aug-2025 one, and resolver counts it)\nlenient = rng.binomial(1, 0.045, N) * rng.binomial(1, 0.55, N)\np_yes_total = np.clip(p_yes + lenient*(1-p_yes), 0, 1)\n\nprint(f\"P(any announcement of genre)  mean = {p_any.mean():.3f}\")\nprint(f\"P(YES) core                   mean = {p_yes.mean():.4f}\")\nprint(f\"P(YES) with lenient allowance mean = {p_yes_total.mean():.4f}\")\nprint(\"percentiles of p_yes_total:\", np.round(np.percentile(p_yes_total,[10,25,50,75,90]),4))\n"

  "code": "\nimport numpy as np, itertools\nrng = np.random.default_rng(11)\nN = 300_000\nwindow = 24/365\n\ndef run(secrecy_mu, activity_mu, both_a, both_b, lenient_p, seed):\n    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    base = r.uniform(0.8, 2.0, N)\n    p_any_base = 1-np.exp(-base*window)\n    act = r.lognormal(np.log(activity_mu), 0.45, N)\n    sec = r.lognormal(np.log(secrecy_mu), 0.45, N)\n    p_any = np.clip(p_any_base*act*sec, 0, 0.95)\n    p_both = r.beta(both_a, both_b, N)\n    p_mat  = r.beta(6, 4, N)\n    core = p_any*p_both*p_mat\n    len_ = r.binomial(1, lenient_p, N)*r.binomial(1, 0.55, N)\n    tot = np.clip(core + len_*(1-core), 0, 1)\n    return p_any.mean(), core.mean(), tot.mean()\n\nprint(f\"{'secrecy':>8}{'activity':>10}{'P(any)':>9}{'core':>9}{'total':>9}\")\nrows=[]\nfor sec_mu in [0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.60]:\n    for act_mu in [1.8, 2.2, 3.0]:\n        a,c,t = run(sec_mu, act_mu, 3.5, 6.5, 0.045, hash((sec_mu,act_mu))%10000)\n        rows.append(t)\n        print(f\"{sec_mu:>8.2f}{act_mu:>10.1f}{a:>9.3f}{c:>9.4f}{t:>9.4f}\")\n\nprint(\"\\nRange of total across grid: %.3f - %.3f, mean %.3f\" % (min(rows), max(rows), np.mean(rows)))\n\n# Also sensitivity on p_both and lenient allowance at central secrecy/activity\nprint(\"\\nSensitivity on p_both mean and lenient prob (secrecy=0.40, activity=2.2):\")\nfor (ba,bb),lab in [((3.5,6.5),'0.35'),((4.5,5.5),'0.45'),((2.5,7.5),'0.25')]:\n    for lp in [0.02, 0.045, 0.08]:\n        a,c,t = run(0.40, 2.2, ba, bb, lp, hash((ba,lp))%10000)\n        print(f\"  p_both~{lab}, lenient={lp:.3f} -> total {t:.4f}\")\n"
}
